paragraphs.text: This divine and great father of ours, Epiphanius, came from Eleutheropolis in Palestine, where he also became a father of monks. For his first ascetic training [?] he withdrew to Egypt, and having stayed there [?] until his return, in the twentieth year of his age he went back again to the district of Eleutheropolis and built a monastery there. The treatise is called Ancoratus, "The Well-Anchored," because like an anchor it steadies the mind that searches into life and salvation. It does so by the comprehensive scope of its treatment of many parts of the faith. I mean the consubstantiality of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit; the complete incarnate coming of Christ; the resurrection of the dead, eternal life and the judgment of flesh and soul together; and, in part, the case against idols and heresies, the Jews and the rest. It also contains the names of the eighty heresies and clarifies other questions in divine Scripture. It was written for the people of Syedra in Pamphylia, who asked for it in the letters placed at the beginning of this treatise. This was done in the ninetieth year from [?], in the tenth year of Valentinian and Valens, and in the sixth [?].

A letter written from Pamphylia, from the city of Syedra, by Tarsinus, Matidius and other presbyters to Epiphanius, bishop of the city of Constantia in Cyprus. In it they asked about the faith in the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit and about other parts of the same faith.
To the lord bishop Epiphanius, honored by God: Matidius, Tarsinus, Neon and Numerianus, presbyters of the catholic church in Syedra, send greetings in the Lord God.

The devil, the enemy of humankind, is accustomed to stir up trouble in various ways. He sows his own seeds among the simpler folk and among those not yet made perfect and firm in the faith of the Holy Trinity. Yet, as it is written, "the firm foundation stands, bearing this seal: The Lord knows those who are his."

The heretics, ready for anything, have now set aside their blasphemy against Jesus and commit impiety against God in another way. They "magnify their tongue" against the Holy Spirit and "speak unrighteousness on high."

Nevertheless, though countless others have been shaken, we ourselves have stood firm in the sound faith by the Lord's grace and have not been moved at all from the right and sound teaching. Many who seemed to have been deceived were also strengthened again by the Lord's grace, through letters from Athanasius, the blessed bishop of worthy memory, and from your most God-fearing fellow minister Proclianus.

But remnants of the evil teaching still linger among some people. You, as experienced husbandmen, must either graft these into the cultivated olive or cut them off entirely. For this reason we write to your Godliness and beg your Reverence to be so good as to write a letter to our church. Please set out the right and sound faith in a fuller account, so that the simpler folk and those still wavering about the faith may be confirmed by your sacred writings, and so that the devil, the enemy of the church, may be put to shame through your holy prayers. We pray to God that you may fare well for many years and remember us in your prayers.
A letter written by Palladius, a civic official of the same city of Syedra, and sent to the same Epiphanius, bishop of Constantia in the island of Cyprus. He too asked about the same matters.
To the master of my soul, the God-honored bishop Epiphanius: Palladius, civic official in Syedra, sends greetings in the Lord God.

People who sail across the great, wide sea pay little attention to the harbors along the shores as long as a gentle wind keeps the ship on course. They expect to bring the vessel across without any trouble.

But when a strong contrary wind strikes them, raising the waves high on every side and swamping the ship, they long for a calm harbor and scan the whole coastline nearby. If they can anchor nowhere, they make for whatever island happens to lie close at hand, seeking safety by any means. Once they reach it and slip into the shelter of its jutting headlands, they are at last barely able to escape the dangers that were flooding over them.

So it is with us now, master. We are being instructed in God's saving word. We are eager to free ourselves from the turmoil of the world and wish to steer our vessel into the unshaken harbor of Christ. But we have learned that some people are raising empty and, it seems to me, irrational questions about the Holy Spirit. They say that he ought not to be glorified together with the Godhead and the Lordship, but has been given the rank of a servant and messenger, and they hold still meaner and lower opinions about him.

For this reason we are caught, as it were, in a restless and grievous storm. We could find no one among us able to resolve these questions and set out the sound faith for us, so we hurried to bring the matter before your Godliness. We may rightly raise this cry ourselves: "Master, save us!"

We therefore appeal to your unfeigned and right faith, which good report has made known ahead of you and which trustworthy witnesses attest and proclaim. You have been appointed by the Savior for this very task. Please receive our request patiently, and be willing to set out the faith of the Holy Trinity in sacred writings, in a fuller and clearer account, and to send it to us. Then we too, confirmed in that faith, may attain what we are striving for; those already well established in it may rejoice; those in error may, if possible, be healed; and "God may be glorified in all things."

A letter written to Pamphylia, to the presbyter Matidius, to Tarantinus, Neon and Numisianus of Syedra, and to Palladius the civic official. It concerns the faith in the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit and other parts of the faith, namely the resurrection of the dead and the incarnation of Christ. It was written in the ninetieth year of Diocletian, in the month of July, in answer to what they asked in their own letters, as those letters state; they are placed at the beginning.

To my lords and most honored brothers and fellow presbyters, Matidius, Tarsinus, [?] and Numerianus, and to all the others with you; and to our most beloved children Palladius and Severianus. You have been zealous with good zeal and [have chosen?] for yourselves the blessed and most desirable life of orthodox faith and complete humility. You fulfill what the Savior said: "If you wish to be perfect, sell your possessions and give to the poor." You also fulfill what was written: "They sold their possessions and laid the proceeds at the apostles' feet." And you devote yourselves to gaining for your own souls whatever is vital and most secure among us. Epiphanius, least of bishops, and the brothers with me send greetings in the Lord God.

I would already count myself blessed, most beloved. We are truly not equal to the virtuous way of life of the saints, of earnest people, and of those who have taken up zeal for God. Yet we are thought worthy to be prompted by these very people to rouse our minds and apply them to what is useful.

Our lowly disposition has always been eager to persevere in quiet and not to reach any further. It pays close attention to the apostle's words: "so that I may not overextend myself beyond the measure of the rule that God has assigned us as our measure." Now, however, it is compelled to take this step.

Votes have prevailed, so to speak, from every side. They come from your God-given zeal and from others who share our belief, that is, those who are zealous for orthodoxy. Among them is our child Hypatius, who came to me from the land of Egypt for this very purpose. These votes have made me lay aside all laziness and all hesitation, so that I no longer keep silent or postpone writing to you about the faith. For you and our brothers are seeking, from the divine and holy Scripture, what concerns our salvation. You want the firm foundation of the faith regarding the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit and the rest of salvation in Christ, namely the resurrection of the dead and the incarnate coming of the Only-begotten. You also ask about the holy covenant, both old and new, and, in a word, about everything else that makes up complete salvation.

I received a presentation of these requests, and they were not few. They came from my fellow presbyter Conops and his followers, from others, and from your honorable selves, most beloved children. Besides that, our child Hypatius came to me from Egypt for this purpose. Seeing so many votes in agreement, I was stung in heart and mind. After reflection I decided to set to work without hesitation, as you asked in your letters. Not only willingly, but even if I had been unwilling, the abundance of requests from you and your people [has brought] me, insignificant as I am, to write this letter in answer to your longing.

2. I am greatly astonished and filled with admiration at the providence of our Lord and God. In the abundance of his goodness he has been pleased to give his Holy Spirit in all things to those who seek him in truth. For I did not consider that your requests by letter, and those of your people, came about without God, most beloved. Rather, I judged that the impulse had its origin in you from the grace of God.

Truly, those who hold orthodox views about the Son of God and the Holy Spirit know how to speak in harmony and agreement with the most blessed apostle Peter: "You are the Christ, the Son of the living God." They will clearly be called blessed by the Lord himself, just as that holy man was blessed when he heard, "Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jona," that is, son of Jonah. For his father was called Jonah, and "bar" translated from the Hebrew language means "son."

For this was the life that the only-begotten Son of God made known to his disciples when he said, "that they may have life in themselves." And this is the life of which he said, "that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent."

By saying "the only true God," then, he led us to the single rule of God. He did this so that we might no longer "be enslaved under the elements of the world" and polytheism might no longer exist among us. Human thoughts should not be scattered into such fornication but should be drawn to the unity of the only true God. For, as Scripture says, "the beginning of fornication is the devising of idols."

And he says, "and Jesus Christ whom you have sent." What is Jesus Christ, if not God? And if Christ Jesus is God, as John says of him, "the only-begotten God, who is in the bosom of the Father, has made him known," then there is one God, the Father, the only true God, and the Only-begotten is also God.

So he is not alien to God or to the divine unity. Because he is the Son from the Father, he is the only true God. He is not like the false gods whom some of the Greeks thought to be gods, though they are not gods. He is the only true God, since he alone is from the One alone, the Only-begotten, and the Holy Spirit is likewise unique. For there is a Trinity in unity, and one God: Father, Son and Holy Spirit.
3. The word alarms those who have not been thought worthy of the Holy Spirit: "For no one can say 'Jesus is Lord' except in the Holy Spirit."

Even the Jews speak the name Jesus, but they do not regard him as Lord. The Arians also speak the name and [call him] God [?], but they say he is God by adoption and not true God, since they have no share in the Holy Spirit.
For unless a person receives the Holy Spirit, he does not call Jesus truly Lord, truly God, truly Son of God and truly eternal King.
Let those who have formed this evil notion learn that the only-begotten Son of God does not bear witness about himself in all things [?].
For this is what he said in the Gospel: "If I bear witness about myself, my testimony is nothing; there is another who bears witness about me."

And who is that other, if not the one who called from heaven, "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased"? Yet the same one who says, "If I bear witness about myself, my testimony is nothing," also says, "Even if I bear witness about myself, my testimony is true." Again he says, "The very works that the Father has given me bear witness about me." And again: "Moses wrote about me," and "Moses bears witness about me."

He first said, "If I bear witness about myself, my testimony is nothing," because many people glorify themselves and bear witness about themselves. He wanted to cut off the boasting of those who boast and commend themselves.

But when he says, "Even if I bear witness about myself, my testimony is true," he shows that the testimony is not that of a mere man. He is God, speaking the truth in his own [testimony?]. Therefore the Father is true God, the Son is true God, and the Holy Spirit is true, since he is "the Spirit of God" and "the Spirit of truth." The Trinity is counted in one name.

For the Son himself says of the Father, "that they may know you, the only true God." And a trustworthy witness about the Son is the disciple who leaned on his breast, who calls him Only-begotten. He did not add "true God" to "only-begotten God"; it is of the Father that Scripture says he is true God, and of the Son that he is "only-begotten God." Conversely, it says of the Father that "[God is] light," and of the Son, "He was the true light."

4. Notice, I ask you, how precise the Scriptures are. The Father is light, yet "true light" is not added where the Father is spoken of. Of the Son, however, it says "true light." Yet no one dares to speak otherwise of the Father.

Who would be so mad, or rather so bent on bringing derangement upon himself, as to dare to incur the suspicion of blasphemy? Who, finding that "true" is not attached to the text, would say of the Father that he is not true light?
For if the genuine Son begotten of him is true light, then the one who begot the Son is beyond doubt true light. He who begot him without beginning and outside time is himself true light.

We must not dare to say of the Father that he is not true light, even though "true" is not added. Through pious understanding we know of ourselves that he is true light, even though it is not written, and we do not doubt it, lest we perish. In the same way, Scripture says of the Son that the Son is God. Even if "true God" is not added, we would heap madness upon ourselves if we dared to blaspheme by refusing to call the Son true God, even though the word is not added.

For it is enough, in the case of one person, to carry over the whole bond of the Trinity, and from the Father to understand the Son as true God and the Spirit as true. Equivalent expressions of truth are set opposite each of the names: "true God" for the Father, "God" for the Son;

and conversely, "the true light" for the Son, "light" for the Father. So we may join the two glories concerning the Godhead: "true God" for the Father and "true light" for the Son, and "light" for the Father and "God" for the Son. From "light" and "God" we may confess the one Godhead, and from "true God" and "true light" the one unity of power.

5. The same is true of the Holy Spirit. "When he comes [?]," he says, "the Spirit of truth." And again he says of himself, "I am the truth." Of the Father there is "the Spirit of my Father who speaks in you." And of the Spirit: "My Spirit stands in your midst."

The Spirit, working ineffably together with the Son, "drives him out into the wilderness" "to be tempted by the devil." And the Lord himself says, "The Spirit of the Lord [is upon me], because he has anointed me."

The Holy Spirit speaks in the prophets: "Thus says the Lord Almighty," and "the Lord who spoke in the prophets." There is also "he who establishes [thunder] and creates wind." He establishes the thunder that resounds among human beings, and he creates the wind that serves the rains God sends upon the earth.

So of created things Scripture says, "he who establishes thunder and creates wind," for these are created. But when it says "announcing his Christ to human beings," it no longer speaks of creating or establishing. It says "announcing him to human beings":

him who was truly begotten of the True, the uncreated, the unchangeable, the unalterable, the ever-existing from the Ever-existing, the one who through Moses [and John?] is shown to be ever-existing [?]. For Moses says, "He Who Is has sent me." And John says, "He who is in the bosom of the Father has made him known."

The Father is "He Who Is," and the Son is "he who is," "he who is with Him Who Is," begotten of him. He is not merged with the Father and did not begin to exist. He is always the genuine Son with the Father, and the Father has always begotten the Son.

For there was never a time when the Father was not Father, and never a time when the Son did not exist for the only Father. For if there was a time when he was not Father, then he himself was the son of another father before he became Father of the Only-begotten.

Those who think they are showing reverence to the Father are utterly impious. For God admits no time, no season, no instant, no indivisible moment of an hour, no twinkling of an eye, no flight of thought. However high

your mind rises to grasp and believe in the Son, it thinks of the Father at the same time. For the name [?] points to the other. If you call him Son, in saying "Son" you think of the Father, for the Father is understood from the Son. And when you say "Father," you signify the Son, for he is necessarily called Father of a Son.

6. When, then, can you dare to say that the Father was not Father, so that you could also dare to say that the Son was not [Son]? And if [one cannot] add dignity to the Father [?] (for the divine exists in unchanging sameness and needs no addition, neither of glory nor of advancement), then "learn not to blaspheme," you who fight against the faith, or rather drive yourself away from the faith. Believe instead in an eternal Father who truly and always begot a Son,
the Son who always truly is, with the Father who truly is.

[?] but begotten. For the Son, always [being with him], is not merged with the Father. He is not a brother, but a genuine Son begotten of the Father, a Son by nature and not by adoption. He is a Son consubstantial with the Father, not [co-existent?] but consubstantial. This means he was not begotten from outside the Father, as some ironically suggest, who want the Son to be Son by adoption and not in truth.
The bond of the faith is to say "consubstantial." If you say "consubstantial," you have broken the power of Sabellius. For where there is "consubstantial," it points to one hypostasis [?];
but it also signifies that the Father has his own subsistence, the Son his own subsistence, and the Holy Spirit his own subsistence.

When someone says "consubstantial," he signifies that the Son is not alien to the same Godhead. He signifies the Son as God from God and the Holy Spirit as God, of the [same?] Godhead, not three gods.
Nor, when we call the Son and the Father God, do we speak of two gods. For our God is one, as blessed Moses says: "The Lord your God, the Lord is one."

We do not speak of gods when we say the Father is God, the Son is God, and the Holy Spirit is God [?], not gods; for there is no plurality of gods in God. Through the three names the one Godhead of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit is signified.

Nor are there two sons. The Son is the one Only-begotten, while the Holy Spirit is Holy Spirit, the Spirit of God. He always exists with the Father and the Son. He is not alien to God but is from God, "proceeding from the Father" and "receiving from" the Son.

The only-begotten Son is incomprehensible, and the Spirit is incomprehensible. The Spirit is from God and is not alien to the Father and the Son. Nor is there a merging of Father and Son. There is a Trinity, always existing, of the same essence. There is no other essence besides the Godhead and no other Godhead besides the essence. It is the same Godhead, and from that same Godhead come the Son and the Holy Spirit.

7. The Holy Spirit is Spirit, and the Son is Son. The Spirit proceeds from the Father and receives from the Son. He "searches the depths of God," announces the things of the Son in the world, and sanctifies the saints through the Trinity. He is third in naming, since the Trinity is the [Father], the Son and the Holy Spirit; for he says, "Go and baptize in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit." He is the seal of grace and the bond of the Trinity. He is not alien to the number, not separated from the naming, not foreign to the gift. Rather, there is one God, one faith, one Lord, one gift of grace, one church, one baptism.
For the Trinity is always Trinity and never receives any addition. It is counted in this way: Father, Son and Holy Spirit.

The Trinity is not a merging, and nothing in it is separated from its own unity. Rather, each subsists in perfection: the Father is perfect, the Son is perfect, the Holy Spirit is perfect, Father, Son and Holy Spirit.

Conversely, the Spirit is listed in connection with the gifts: "For there are varieties of gifts, but the same Spirit; there are varieties of ministries, but the same Lord; and there are varieties of workings, but the same God who works all things in all."

Let us not stray from the subject before us or depart from the truth. We are not advocates pleading on God's behalf. We seek to understand piously, lest we perish, and we speak not as those who fully comprehend. As human beings, we speak what we have grasped.
For the honor due to God is infinite, and [the Trinity] [?] ten thousand times beyond our mind. It takes on no addition of glory, and none of its distinctive properties is taken away.

For nothing in the Trinity is created or came into being later. The Father begets the Son, and there was never a time when the Son did not exist. Nor was the Father at any time not called Father. He was always Father, and the Son always existed. The Son is not a brother but a Son, begotten in a way that cannot be told and named in a way beyond comprehension. He is always with the Father and never ceases to exist.

The Father, then, is unbegotten, uncreated and incomprehensible. The Son is begotten, yet uncreated and incomprehensible. The Holy Spirit is eternal: not begotten, not created, not a brother, not an uncle, not an ancestor, not an offspring. He is the Holy Spirit, from the same essence as the Father and the Son. For "God is spirit."
8. Each of the names is unique; none of them is duplicated. For the Father is Father and has no counterpart, nor is he paired with another father, lest there be two gods.

And the Son is only-begotten, true God from true God. He does not bear the name of Father, nor is he estranged from the Father; he is the Son of the Father. He is only-begotten so that the Son may bear a unique name, and God from God so that Father and Son may be called one God. And the Holy Spirit is one and only, not
bearing the name of Son or the title of Father, but called simply Holy Spirit, and not alien to the Father.

For the Only-begotten himself speaks of "the Spirit of the Father," and "who proceeds from the Father," and "he will take what is mine," so that he would not be thought alien to the Father or to the Son, but of the same essence and the same Godhead: divine Spirit, "the Spirit of truth," the Spirit of God, the Spirit the Paraclete. He is called by a unique name, has no counterpart, and is not equated with any other spirit. He is not called by the name of Son or by the title of Father, so that the unique names may not become shared names;
except that "God" is said in the Father, "God" in the Son, and in the Holy Spirit "of God" and "God" [?].

For he is the Spirit of God, the Spirit of the Father and the Spirit of the Son. This is not by some kind of composition, as soul and body are in us. He is in the midst of Father and Son, from the Father and the Son, third in naming.

For he says, "Go and baptize in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit." The Father baptizes into his own name, into the name of God, and the seal stamped on us in the name of God is perfect. Christ baptizes into his own name, into the name of God, and the seal stamped on us in the name of God is perfect. If that is so, who will dare to wage war against his own soul by calling the Spirit alien to the Godhead?

For if we are sealed into the name of the Father, into the name of the Son, and into that of the Holy Spirit, there is one seal of the Trinity, and therefore one power of the Godhead in the Trinity. But if the one is God and the others are created and not God, on what principle are the two bound to the one in the seal of perfection? Have we, then, been sealed into a single royal name, the Father's, while the others are not royal? [?] Are we still enslaved to elements and creatures? Was the Father's name alone unable to save? Did he, as the blasphemers suppose, create two further elements and take them to himself, so that his Godhead might acquire additional powers? Was it only so that he could save the one sealed by him, and so that the human being he created could receive redemption through the forgiveness of sins?

9. Alas for such drivel! Oh, such blasphemy! Where has this new unbelief crept into the world from — or rather, should I say, this misbelief? For misbelief is worse than unbelief. Unbelief is set right once it receives faith, but misbelief cannot be corrected and is saved only with difficulty, unless perhaps the anointing comes upon it from above.
So the blessed Peter says to Ananias and his companions, "Why has Satan tempted you to lie to the Holy Spirit?" And he says, "You have not lied to men, but to God."

Therefore the Spirit, to whom those who kept back part of the price lied, is God from Father and Son. Paul too agrees with this when he says, "You are the temple of God, and the Spirit of God dwells in you." So then the Spirit is God, as I said before.

That is why holy people, who have the Holy [Spirit] of God dwelling in them, will be called the temple of God. The very chief of the apostles testifies to this. The Lord counted him worthy to be called blessed because the Father had revealed it to him.
So the Father reveals the true Son to him, and he is called blessed; and the same Father again reveals his Holy Spirit.

It was fitting [?] that the first of the apostles, the firm rock, "on which the church of God is built, and the gates of Hades shall not prevail against it" — and the gates of Hades are the heresies and the heresiarchs. For in every way the faith was made firm in him, who received the key of heaven, who looses on earth and binds in heaven.
For in him all the subtle points of the faith that people seek are found.

This is the man who denied three times and cursed three times before the cock crowed. To show how great his love for his own Master was, he had insisted, "Even if all deny you, I will not deny you," saying as much as lay in him [?]. This is the man who wept at the crowing

of the cock. He did so in order to confess truly that the arrest of the Son of God was not in appearance but real, and so to declare him a true man by weeping over his arrest when he was handed over by the Pharisees. This is the man who went away to Galilee [?] to fish,
the companion of the one who reclined on the Lord's breast. That disciple learned from the Son, received from the Son, and revealed the power of knowledge, while this one was taught by the Father,

laying the foundation of the faith's security. It was he who fished again in the boat on the Lake of Tiberias after he had been called. The Savior said, "Children, do you have anything to eat?" and then, "Cast to the right side of the boat and you will find." Peter was astonished at what happened at that word, and the disciple whom Jesus loved, John, said to him, "It is the Lord": man according to the flesh, truly born of Mary and not in appearance, but God according to

[?] being, having come from heaven, from the Father. This is the man who heard from him, "Peter, feed my lambs." He was entrusted with the flock and guides it well in the power of his own Master. He confesses the truth about the flesh and faithfully proclaims what the Father revealed about the Son. He points to the Spirit and to his dignity in the Godhead. Together with James and John he gave Paul and Barnabas the right hand of fellowship, so that "by three witnesses every word may be established."

10. For nothing can stand without two or three witnesses. By these the faith too was confirmed in a riddle through the Law, for those who knew only the Father. They could not be filled unless they received the power of the Son, were strengthened by the witness of Father and Son, and through the third witness received the Holy Spirit,
as the voices of the cherubim and seraphim plainly cry out the threefold "Holy, holy, holy."

For the doxology in heaven is not completed with two voices. These holy, invisible spiritual living creatures do not cry out a fourth time or raise a fourth voice, nor do they use only one. They use three voices in the singular: "Holy, holy, holy."

And they do not say "Holy ones, holy ones," lest they declare the singular to be many-named, or [?] the number of the three. They offer the hallowing three times, but they utter the word in a single form and in the singular, so as not to proclaim many gods.

For God is one: the Father in the Son, the Son in the Father, with the Holy Spirit. And for this reason he is "the Holy One who rests among the holy." The Father truly exists in his own person, the Son truly exists in his own person, and the Holy Spirit truly exists in his own person. Though they are three, they are one Godhead, one essence, one glory, one God.

If you have named the Son, your mind has embraced the Trinity. If you have the Holy Spirit, you have been counted worthy of the Father's power and of the Son of God. If you have glorified the Father, you have also pointed to the Son and the Holy Spirit.

Yet they are not blended together. For the Father is Father, the Son is Son, and the Holy Spirit is Holy Spirit. But the Trinity is not estranged from its unity and identity. The Father is honored as Father; the Son is honored as Son; the Holy Spirit is honored as true Spirit and Spirit of God. So the Only-begotten says, "He who honors the Father honors the Son"; for when you speak of the Father you point to the Son and honor the Son. And "He who honors the Son honors the Father"; for when you name the Son you honor the Father, provided you do not declare Christ less than the Father.

11. Even among us humans such an attitude is absent: we do not want our sons to be inferior or to fall short of the honor their fathers enjoy (for dishonor done to sons reflects on the fathers in equal measure). How much more, then, would God the Father not wish his own Son to be diminished?
So whoever supposes that the true Son of the Father falls short of the Father's glory, carried along by ignorance, dishonors the [Father] instead of honoring [him] [?].

So the Son reveals the Father when he says, "No one knows the Father except the Son, and no one knows the Son except the Father." In the same way, I dare to say, no one knows the Spirit either, except the Father and the Son, from whom he proceeds and from whom he receives.

How do they dare to call the Spirit alien to God, these men who are possessed by madness rather than by truth? They do not learn from the true words of the trustworthy and holy apostle Paul. Peter, the very chief of the apostles, counted worthy to hold the key of the kingdom, gave Paul his right hand. Paul heard from heaven, "Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?";

he was counted worthy to hear "unspeakable words, which no one may utter"; and he says, "No one knows the things of a man except the spirit of the man that dwells in him." He wished to describe the things above by means of an illustration. His aim was not to make God like the human example, but to reveal through the illustration a part of the things above.

For if the whole creation were gathered together — angels and archangels, cherubim and seraphim with the heavenly host, heaven and earth, things on earth, in heaven and under the earth, luminaries and stars, land and sea, and in short everything in heaven and on earth — it could not be shown to be like its Master, nor be likened to him by any comparison.
For he grants the image to man by grace, as Scripture says: "God made man; in the image of God he made him." Every human being has the image as a gift of grace,

but no one will be made like his Master. For the one is invisible, the other visible; the one immortal, the other subject to death. The one is the fountain of all wisdom and has all things perfect in himself. Man has a gift only in part and falls short of what is most perfect, unless God wills to grant those who receive it, according to their worth, the perfection that comes through grace.

12. Nevertheless, the same holy apostle makes use of an illustration and says, "No man knows the things of a man except the spirit of the man that dwells in him; so also no one has known the things of God";
and he did not say, "except the Spirit of God that dwells in him," but only "the Spirit of God," so that no one would think of the divine as composite and made up of parts.
"Except," he says, "the Spirit of God"; "for the Spirit of God searches all things, even the depths of God."

So the Spirit of God, who searches the depths of God, is not alien to him. The divine Scripture rebukes us when it says, "Think about what you have been commanded, for you have no need of hidden things," and "Do not seek what is too high for you, and do not examine what is too deep for you." Are we then to say the same of the Spirit, that [?] he searches the depths of God improperly? Would that not rather be absurd?
For why does he search the depths of God? For what reason? Tell me, you fool: as a busybody? As one who meddles in others' affairs? As one who craves what is not his own? God forbid!

Rather, the saints are counted worthy to have the Holy Spirit dwell in them. When the Holy Spirit comes to be in the saints, he grants them to search the depths of God. The purpose is that they may glorify God deeply (David too confesses this: "Out of the depths," he says, "I have cried to you, O Lord"). They are to glorify him as infinitely good, and not in a mean and paltry way, like those of the heresy of Arius and all the heresies outside the church.

From the time [?] the Law was given through Moses, eleven heresies split off after him before Christ's coming in the flesh, and another sixty after his coming in the flesh. This is apart from those before the Law: the five of all these, and the other four Greek heresies, which make nine before the Law. Altogether, together with their mothers, they number eighty.
The mothers among them are these five: Barbarism, Scythism, Hellenism, Judaism and Samaritanism. From Hellenism come four heresies: the Pythagoreans, the Platonists, the Stoics and the Epicureans.

From the Law, before Christ's coming in the flesh, came eleven. Seven came from the Jews: the Scribes, Pharisees, Sadducees, Ossaeans, Nasaraeans, Hemerobaptists and Herodians. Four came from the Samaritans: the Gorothenes, Sebuaeans, Essenes and Dositheans. Altogether eleven sprang from the Law, out of the Jews and the Samaritans.

13. So all the heresies before Christ's coming in the flesh, beginning from Adam and continuing up to that coming, are twenty. After Christ's coming in the flesh, up to the reign of Valentinian, Valens and Gratian, all the heresies that have falsely claimed the name of Christ for themselves number sixty. They are counted as follows:

[Simonians?] [?], Menandrians, Saturnilians, Basilidians, Nicolaitans, Gnostics (also called Stratiotics and Phibionites, by some Secundians, by others Socratites, by others Zacchaeans, by some Coddians, and also Borborites), Carpocratians, Cerinthians (also called Merinthians), Nazoraeans, [Ebionites?] [?], Valentinians, Secundians (with whom Epiphanes and Isidore are joined), Ptolemaeans, Marcosians, Colorbasians, Heracleonites, Ophites, Cainites, Sethians, Archontics, Cerdonians, Marcionites, Lucianists, Apelleans, Severians, Tatianists, Encratites, Phrygians (also called Montanists and Tascodrugites), Pepuzians (also called Priscillianists and Quintillianists, with whom the Artotyrites are joined), Quartodecimans (who keep Easter on a single day of the year), Alogi (who do not accept the Gospel and the Revelation of John), [Adamians?] [?], Sampsaeans (also called Elkesaites), Theodotians, Melchizedekians, Bardesanists, Noetians, Valesians, Cathari (also called Novatians, and Montenses as they are called in Rome), Angelics, Apostolics (also called Apotactics), Sabellians, Origenists (also called the Shameful), the Origenists of Adamantius, the heresy of Paul of Samosata, Manichaeans (also called Acuanites), Hieracites, Melitians (who are a schism in Egypt), Arians (also called Ariomanites), the schism of the Audians (a schism but not a heresy), Photinians, Marcellians, Semi-Arians, Pneumatomachians (who blaspheme the Holy Spirit of God), Aerians [?], Aetians (also called Anomoeans, to whom Eunomius is joined — or rather the lawless one), Dimoerites (who do not confess Christ's incarnation as complete), also called Apollinarians, those who say that holy Mary was united with Joseph after she had given birth to the Savior (whom we have called Antidicomarianites), those who offer a cake in her name (who are called Collyridians), and Messalians, with whom are joined the Martyrians, who come from the Greeks, the Euphemites and the Satanians.
14. I have grown utterly weary, and am still weary, of counting up the names of so many heresies and recounting their lawless deeds, and those of the two schisms besides.

I mean, first, the Melitians in Egypt mentioned above. They split themselves off because of certain people who fell during the persecution and whom our side, after their repentance, received back into their clerical ranks.

Yet they are not in heresy. I mean also the Audians in Mesopotamia, likewise mentioned above, who are also a schism and not a different faith. They merely quarrel, in an uneducated way, over what being "in the image" means. They have not rebelled over the faith or separated themselves for any other reason, but out of a self-chosen extremity of supposed righteousness. They refuse communion with bishops and presbyters who possess gold and silver, and they keep the Passover at the time when the Jews keep it. For these reasons they cut themselves off and estrange themselves from the unity of the orthodox church.

For those who did not receive the Holy Spirit did not learn the depths of God. They were broken off into these heresies and into the schisms on the pretext of petty disputes. For they abandoned the truth and went down many paths, thinking now one thing and now another.

The same holy apostle shows us why he said this: "But we have received the Spirit of God, so that we may know the things freely given to us by God. These we also speak, not in words taught by wisdom, but in words taught by the Holy Spirit, comparing spiritual things with spiritual," and so on. The Spirit of God, then, is not alien to God. For if he is alien to God, how does he search the depths of God?

But what will you say to me, you vainglorious man, who are waging war against yourself — I would rather not say against the Holy Spirit of God? Why, vainglorious man, do you wage war against the invincible? Why fight the unconquerable? "It is hard for you to kick against the goads." You cause yourself to stumble, not the Word. You ensnare yourself, not the Spirit. You estrange yourself from the grace of God, but you do not estrange the Son from the Father, nor the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son.

15. No doubt you will say, cleverly — for I have already heard some arrogant people twisting the truth of our God and Savior into blasphemy — "He searches the depths of God, but does not comprehend them." They say this because that word is not attached to the text. The apostle said only "searches the depths of God"; "comprehends" is not added.
What utter stupidity! Was there any need, you wretch driven by God's wrath, to say "comprehends" after saying "searches"? Would the statement, in your ignorance, be lame without that word?

But now you are left with no excuse. For Scripture gathers the truth from every side for the most devout man. Of God Almighty it is written: "God who tests the kidneys and searches the chambers of the belly." If he tests the kidneys, does he not know what he is testing?

Or did Scripture place the whole of his knowledge in the testing? "And searches the chambers of the belly" — again, "comprehending" is not added. So, because "comprehends" is not added to the text, am I to bring death upon myself by weaving "does not comprehend" into it, as your reasoning requires, you fool?

So too it is said of the Holy Spirit that he searches, and there was no need to say that he also comprehends. The word itself shows that the knowledge of God and of the depths of God is in the Holy Spirit. Even though it does not say "comprehends," understand it to mean the same, and do not destroy your own soul.

No one should dare to say of the Father that he searches and does not comprehend. For he created man together with the Son and the Holy Spirit, and the Trinity is always a Trinity and never receives any addition. In the same way, the same must be understood of the Holy Spirit.

For when he says, "Let us make man" (for "In the beginning God made heaven and earth"), it signifies the Father's voice summoning others to the work of creation. And in saying "Let us make," I would say it signifies not only the Son but also the Holy Spirit.

For thus it says: "By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and all their host by the breath of his mouth." So the Word creates together with the Father, and the Holy Spirit also creates together with him.

Does God Almighty, then, who made man, not know the things of man, though he "searches the chambers of the belly"? On the contrary, Scripture adds this to express the fullness of God's knowledge, so that none of us who sin may think that anything is hidden from God. For he knows man and the things of man.

16. So the Father searches the chambers of the belly, and knows; the Spirit searches the depths of God, and knows. For he reveals the mysteries of God to the saints, teaches them to glorify God deeply, and shows his own the incomprehensibility of God.

So the Spirit is not alien to God. For Scripture did not say of the angels, nor of the archangels, that they search the depths of God. "For no one knows the day or the hour," says the Son of God, "neither the angels of heaven nor the Son, but only the Father."

But the fools, who are not adorned with the Holy Spirit, think that there is something in the Father that is not in the Godhead of the Son. [?] "For as the Father has life in himself, so the Son has life in himself," and "All that is my Father's is mine," says the same holy Word of God.

And what are the things of the Father? That the Father is God belongs also to the Son. The Father's life belongs also to the Son. The Father's light is clearly the Son's as well. The Father's immortality is likewise the Son's. The Father's incomprehensibility is also the Son's.
All that belongs to the Father belongs to the Son. If, then, what is the Father's is his, the knowledge that is in the Father exists also in the Son and in the Holy Spirit.

But if anyone thinks that the Son does not know the day, let the ignorant man learn and not blaspheme. For I offer him knowledge, and he will know. Tell me, beloved — for I call you beloved, since I hate no one except the devil, the works of the devil, and misbelief. I pray for you, that you may come to the truth of God and not destroy yourself by blaspheming God.

For the words of the holy God are deep, and knowledge is given by the Holy Spirit through his gifts. "For to one," it says, "is given a word of wisdom, to another a word of teaching," and so on, "but it is the same Spirit who distributes to each as he wills." He says this to show you the sovereign authority of the Holy Spirit as well.

For when the same Spirit gives the gifts as he wills — then pray to the Father to reveal the Son to you, and pray to the Son to reveal the Father to you. Pray to the Father again to give you the Son, to reveal the Holy Spirit to you, and to grant you to have him within you. Then the Holy Spirit, given within you, may reveal to you all the knowledge of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, so that you may learn that there is no ignorance whatever in the Son, nor in the Holy Spirit.

17. For even if angels fall short of the greater authority and knowledge, God forbid that the Son of God and his Holy Spirit should also fall short. The Son, the holy Word who came to us from the Father, speaks spiritually; but the merely natural are judged, because they do not understand the wisdom of the Son, or rather the meaning of that wisdom. I put a question to you, and you tell me:

Which is greater, the Father or that day of which he speaks? You will not dare to say that the Father is not greater. If, then, the Father is greater than the day and the hour and all things that have come into being and will come into being through him, and no one knows him except the Son, which is the greater thing: to know the Father, or to know that day? Clearly, to know the Father. How then can one who knows the greater things fall short in the lesser?
If, then, he knows the Father, he certainly knows the day as well, and there is nothing in which the Son falls short in knowledge.

But you will say that the Father, being greater, has knowledge of all things, while the Son by no means does, just as he himself says, "My Father is greater than I." But the Son says this to honor the Father, as was fitting, since he himself has been honored all the more greatly by the Father. For truly the genuine son had to honor his own father, so as to show that he was genuine.

But in what way do you suppose he is greater? In extent, or bulk, or time, or season, or rank, or deity, or immortality, or eternity? Do not suppose any of these. For nothing in the Godhead is unequal with respect to the Son; rather, inasmuch as the Father is Father, and inasmuch as the Son is a genuine Son, he honors his own Father.

For the divine is not a matter of bulk, so that the Father should be bulkier than the Son; nor is it subject to time, so that the Father should be beyond the Son in time; nor is the Father located in some part on high (for he contains all things, while he himself is contained by nothing), so that the Son should be thought of as surpassed. For he sat at the right hand of the Father, and Scripture did not say, "he entered into the Father," so as to undo Sabellius and to bring Arius down from his blasphemy.

18. Therefore do not seek what is not to be sought, but honor the Son, so that you may honor the Father. And when you hear it said of God, "No one is good but God alone," do not dare to declare the Son not good because the Son honors the Father so surpassingly.

For it is not by denying that he himself is good that he calls the Father good. Rather, he reveals himself all the more greatly by not wishing to receive honor from men, but referring the honor to his own Father, so that from the goodness of the Father the goodness of the Son of God might be known, since he was begotten of a good Father, God.
For great is the feebleness of those who dare to say such a thing about the Son, even though he says, "One is good, God."

For see how in many places divine Scripture teaches us, calling a poor and wise youth good, and saying, "Samuel was good with God and men," and "Saul son of Kish, of the tribe of Benjamin, was good, taller than all Israel from the shoulders upward," and "It is good to go to the house of drinking," and "Open, O Lord, the heaven, your good treasury," and "A good word is better than a gift," and "A living dog is good, rather than a dead lion," and "Two are good, rather than one," and "The end of words is good, rather than the beginning," and "If you, who are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children," where he is speaking of fish and bread.
How then do you dare to imagine that the Son is denying his own goodness, and not that, out of an excess of honor, he is referring the goodness to the

Father? For he saw that the man who said to him, "Good teacher," was speaking with his mouth and not with his heart. He wished to reprove him, because he did not trust the man's lips but searched his heart, as he also says in another place, "Why do you call me 'Lord, Lord,' and do not do what I say?" So here too he wished to reprove him. For the man called him a good teacher, yet did not abide in his faith so as to believe in his [?]

19. He himself, then, is the holy Word: the living, the subsistent, the heavenly King, the genuine Son, who is always with the Father, who came forth from [?], "the radiance of his glory, the exact imprint of his being," the "image of the Father" in truth, who shares the throne of the one who begot him, "of whose kingdom there will be no end," "the judge of the living and the dead,"

who is Wisdom from Wisdom, who is a Spring from the Spring (for he says, "They have forsaken me, the spring of the water of life, and have dug for themselves broken cisterns"), the ever-flowing river that "makes glad the city of God with its streams," who came forth from the Spring, from whom, as it is written,
"rivers will flow from his belly"; the scepter of David, the root of Jesse, the flower that springs from it, the lion, the king from the tribe of Judah,

the rational lamb, the living stone, the "angel of great counsel," who truly became man and truly is God, not changed in nature, not having altered the Godhead, who was born in the flesh, the incarnate Word.

The Word who became flesh: who has "flesh" between "the Word" and "became" (for Scripture did not say, "the Word who became"; but after saying "the Word," it places "flesh" with no verb, and after "flesh" it says "became," so that the "became" may be shown to be from Mary, and so that the Word may be understood to have come down from above, from the Father). This holy, living Word, God with the Father,

the "angel of great counsel," who announces the Father's counsel, "the father of the age to come," himself said, "No one knows the day and the hour, not even the angels in heaven." [?] For indeed the angels do not know; and it is with a deeper meaning that the Son says, "except the Father alone."

If, then, the Son knows the Father, and the Father is greater than both the day and the hour, which no one doubts, how can one who knows the greater be ignorant of the lesser? For no one knows the Father except the Son, and no one knows the Son except the Father. For just as the Father is great because he knows the Son, so too the Son is great because he knows the Father.

If, then, he knows the Father, the greater, how can he be ignorant of the small, that is, the day and the hour? Search the Scriptures and learn the power of the Holy Spirit, and the Spirit himself, who knows the Father and the Son, will reveal to you the knowledge of the Word, the Son of God, so that you may not stray from the truth and lose your own soul.

20. For there are two kinds of knowledge in divine Scripture, two kinds of knowing: one by action and one by perception. And so that I may set out parallel cases from examples, so that your mistaken mind, and the minds of those who think as you do, may be set straight by many of them,
learn what Scripture says about Adam: "They were naked in paradise," it says, "and were not ashamed."

Yet they were not blind; they could see. For if they could not see, how did they see that the tree was "good for food and beautiful to look upon"? And "the woman took of it," it says, "and ate, and gave also to her husband who was with her."

So they were not blind, but had their eyes open. Though naked, they were not ashamed, even though they could see; and being naked, they knew each other. But they knew each other by perception, not by action.
After they had eaten of the tree and been cast out of paradise, after a long time, it says, "Adam knew Eve his wife." How then can this be?
And yet they had seen each other naked and knew each other by sight, but not by action. It is their union with each other that Scripture called knowing.

Scripture knows how to use the word "knowing" in two senses [?]. For again it says, "Jacob knew Leah his wife, and she conceived and bore a son." Even before this he knew her, for he had been with her for seven years while tending the sheep of Laban her father. He knew her with the knowing that comes through sight and acquaintance; he knew her

also through action. And "he knew Rachel his wife." And again in another place it says, "David grew old, and they covered him with garments, but he did not grow warm; and they said to the king, 'Let a beautiful virgin be sought.'" And Abishag the Shunammite was found. And it says, "She was brought to the king, and she lay with him and kept him warm; and David did not know her," though she was with him, body to body and side by side.

So which kind of knowing does it mean? The knowing through sight, or the knowing through action? And "The Lord knew those who are his": does he then not know those who are not his? And "Depart from me, you workers of lawlessness; I never knew you": is there then ignorance in the Son of God?
And again: "You alone have I known out of all the nations." Does he then not know the other nations? God forbid! Rather, divine Scripture knows one knowing by perception and another by action.

21. Since, then, the Only-begotten, fulfilling the Father's will [?], has already shown all things to be accomplished [?]: the Father knew the hour and the day, and knew it both by knowledge and by action. For he knows all things. And when the Son says, "The Father has given all judgment to the Son," the Father, though he does not judge, himself judges through having given judgment to the Son. For God is not estranged from judging those who are judged, and in the Father's not judging he has already judged.

But the Son knows when he is coming; for he himself brings the day, and he himself appoints it, summons it and brings it to completion. For it says, "That day comes like a thief in the night"; and it says, "You are not in the night, that the day should overtake you in darkness."

If, then, the servants of Christ are children of the day, is the Son himself, who brings the day, ignorant of it, so that the day overtakes him, rather than his bringing the day? Who, thinking such things, will not fall into blasphemy, attributing to the Father and the Son what is unfitting?

So the Father knows the day and the hour in two ways, by perception and by action. For he knows when it is coming, and he has also already judged, having appointed [?] to judge, and so he has known it by action.

The Son of God knows when it is coming; he himself brings it, and he is not ignorant of it. But he has not yet carried it out in knowledge, that is, he has not yet known it by action. For the ungodly still act ungodly, unbelievers still disbelieve, the perverse still blaspheme, the devil is at work, sins are committed, injustice prevails, and judgment waits patiently, until he comes and knows it by action, executes vengeance, and saves those who truly hope in him and do not blaspheme his Godhead and that of the Father and the Holy Spirit.

22. But in the holy angels such dignity falls short in two ways. They are indeed honored, having received this honor from the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. Yet they lack this: they do not know when the things appointed will take place. For the Father has set the times by his own authority. But if the Father is in the Son and the Son in the Father, then the authority that is in the Father is not lacking to the Son.
But it is lacking to the angels. For angels, archangels and powers are created, but the Father is uncreated, the Son uncreated, the Spirit of God uncreated.

The angels, then, know the day and the hour neither by perception nor by action. For they do not know when the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit will choose to bring the day; nor do they know it by the knowledge of action, for they have not yet been commanded to go out, gather people like tares, and bind them in bundles to be burned with unquenchable fire.

So they have neither yet acted nor do they know. The Father both knows and has acted; the Son knows, but has not yet acted. This is the meaning of "except the Father alone, neither the angels nor the Son."

Let us understand the force of Scripture, so that the letter may not become death to us. "For the letter," it says, "kills, but the Spirit gives life." Let us take hold of the Spirit, so that we may benefit from the letter. For it is not the letter that kills, since life is in the letter. Rather, it kills the one who approaches the letter without understanding and does not have the Spirit who explains it, who opens up the letter and reveals what is in it.

This holy Father, then, gave his only-begotten, genuine Son, begotten of him, and his Holy Spirit to his holy church, in one knowledge of concord, in one bond of perfection, so that we might receive the seal in the name of the Father, perfect and God, and receive the seal in the name of the Son, perfect and God, and in the name of the Spirit, divine and perfect.

O holy Trinity, numbered! A Trinity numbered in one name! For it is not called a one and a two, nor a unit and a unit, but a Unity in Trinity and a Trinity in Unity, of one form and one name, one God: the Father in the Son, the Son in the Father, with the Holy Spirit.

23. Call me witnesses of the truth. Call me the youths who were saved from the Babylonian furnace, who were deemed worthy to be thrown into the fire and not consumed. God did not quench the fire, so that they would not be thought to have contrived some novel counter-device; rather, they were in the fire and yet were not consumed by the fire, because of their right faith. Through them God teaches us which things are created and which uncreated, which are made and which did not come into being, which exist eternally and which come from them and have come into being.

These youths, saved in this way, wished to show a grateful mind toward the God who had saved them, in whom they had hoped from the beginning. They did not waver, nor did they bow their necks to the image, to the king's arrogance or to his tyranny.

And when they wished to render something to God, being holy, they searched the depths in their hearts by the Holy Spirit. They considered the heaven and all that is in it, the earth and all that is beneath it, and all that exists, and found these unworthy to be presented to God as an offering (for they had no authority to offer God things beyond themselves).

They wished, in keeping with their rank and authority, simply to praise God with hymns (for this is what is written: "Offer a sacrifice of praise," and "A sacrifice of praise will glorify me"). Prompted by the Holy Spirit, they had already changed the old covenant into the new, and had no need of animal sacrifices or whole burnt offerings (for they say, "There is no place to offer firstfruits, nor sacrifice, nor altar," since all things had been taken in).

Wishing to offer such praise and acknowledging their own smallness, they bore themselves humbly ("For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and he who humbles himself will be exalted"; for along with the gift of their salvation they received this further gift of humility). They wished to offer praise to God and not to lose heart.

Having tested themselves against the ineffable glorification of God, they thought it right to take creation along with them in glorifying him, and they began to speak, embracing the whole of creation.
24. Distinguishing the things made from the Maker, and the things created from the Creator, they say, "Bless the Lord, all you works of the Lord." They said "all" and left nothing out.

And so that the Holy Spirit might mark out the perfect knowledge by which we know what is divine and what has been made by God, so that we might not mix what came into being out of nothing with the eternal, and so that we might not lose our understanding, he gathered all things together by number.

For the Holy Spirit revealed to them, since they were deemed worthy to be with the angels, having become like angels [?], the things in heaven and on earth and under the earth; and from then on they were not ignorant of them.

And these same holy ones say, as I said before, "Bless the Lord, all you works of the Lord," and they begin to enumerate and distinguish which are the works and which is the one who made them, which is the one who works and which are the things worked:

they enumerate the heaven, the earth, the waters above the heaven, and angels (for angels are created), and thrones and powers (for these are created), sun and moon (for these are made and not uncreated), clouds and snowfalls, winds, snows, lightnings, thunders, earth, sea, springs, deeps, rivers, all humankind, mountains, birds of the air, cattle and beasts, souls of the holy, spirits of the righteous, Ananias, Azarias, Misael, priests and servants of God.

For all these are made and created, having come into being from God through the Word and the Holy Spirit: "For by the word of the Lord the heavens were made firm, and by the Spirit of his mouth all their power."

But see, beloved brother, how they enumerated all things, borne along by the Holy Spirit, yet did not number the Son among the things made, nor the Holy Spirit either. Rather, they knew that the same Godhead is in the Trinity and the same Trinity is in one Godhead. And they glorified the Father in the Son and the Son in the Father, with the Holy Spirit: one holiness, one worship, one Godhead, one glorification.

25. But the devil certainly dares to stir up this too among people: an audacious unbelief that tells lies against the holy youths and says, "They did not know how to speak the name of the Holy Spirit. For they were Jews, and being Jews they did not know the Son either."

But the words themselves at once refute the unbelief of the heterodox. For it says, "And the appearance of the fourth was like the appearance of a son of God." See, here is the name of the Son of God, so there is no ignorance about this. [?] And even before the time of the furnace, Daniel was filled with the Holy Spirit and said, "I am innocent of her blood," and "they returned to the court," and he judged the elders, filled with the Holy Spirit.

So they knew the Son, and they knew the Father and the Holy Spirit. It was not out of ignorance that they did not speak the names, but for safety's sake. For it says, "Bless the Lord, all you works of the Lord"; they did not say, "Son of God, bless the Lord," nor "Holy Spirit, bless the Lord," but "Bless the Lord, all you works of the Lord."

And let none of those who hunt for pretexts for themselves say, "They did not mention the Cherubim or the Seraphim, so these are not works of God either." For the divine word anticipated them and secured everything against [?] those who devise schemes for themselves, foreknowing the outrage they would commit against the youths.

For the holy youths repeated the hymn in threefold fashion, the same youths who brought forward the created and made things to hymn God. First they said, "Blessed are you, O Lord, God of our fathers, and praised and glorified is your name forever"; then, after other things, "Blessed are you who sit upon the Cherubim"; and again, "Blessed are you who sit on the throne of the glory of your kingdom"; and "Blessed are you who behold the deeps, seated upon the Cherubim."

They did this so that from the mention of the throne you might understand the Seraphim and Cherubim, and so that from the names of the Cherubim, the deeps, the hallowed throne and all the other names, and from the enumeration of everything named, you might understand that these belong to the works and are numbered along with the rest. For having called all these to the hymn, they immediately add, "Bless the Lord, all you works of the Lord," so that Gabriel and Michael might bless the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit.

26. The august angels in heaven sing the hymn of victory together with the Seraphim and Cherubim. They glorify the Trinity as equal in glory, equal in rank and one in substance, saying "Holy, holy, holy": they complete three utterances, yet say them in unity and not with many names.

For they do not say "holy" a fourth time, so as not to add to the naming of the Trinity; they do not say "holy" only twice, so that the glory of perfection may not be deficient; but they say it three times, so as to hallow the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit with the same honor.
And they do not say "holy" and "half-holy," but say "holy" equally each time. With one voice, one word and one perfection they glorify the Trinity together in unity and the unity in Trinity.

For this is the knowledge that the only-begotten Son of God came to [?] us; this is the understanding the Holy Spirit proclaimed to us; this is the perfection the Father revealed to us in truth; this is the life the incarnate Word bestowed on us; this is the building the Holy Spirit built for us.

"For if anyone builds on this foundation with gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, straw," and so on [?]. For there is no other foundation: "For no one can lay any foundation other than the one already laid, which is Jesus Christ," the Son of God, "whose building we are, and whose field we are," "built on the foundation of the prophets and apostles." This is so that we may know that our building is truly firm, and that our foundation always exists and never began to be.
But "not everyone has this knowledge," in the apostle's words, but only those who have been deemed worthy by the Holy Spirit to know the mysteries of the truth.

For he himself, who revealed himself, his own Father and the Holy Spirit, rebuked some of those in ignorance, saying, "You know neither the Scriptures nor their power"; and again elsewhere, "Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear"; and again he said to the Samaritan woman, "If you knew who it is that asks you for a drink, you would have asked him"; and again, "You do not know what spirit you are of."

So then, "not everyone has this knowledge"; for "each has different gifts from God." And the holy word says, "To whom more is given, from him they will demand more," since some receive little, some nothing at all, and others have received more abundantly.

27. That this is so can be found from what is said in the divine Scriptures themselves. The divine Scripture speaks spiritually for the most part, especially about our life, by which I mean the knowledge of the Lord. So the words that are deeper, and that most surely make our soul secure, have turned out to be a stumbling block to those who have not grasped the knowledge of God,

as the prophet Hosea says: "Who is wise, and will understand these things?" and "The one to whom a word of the knowledge of the Lord is given will know them. For the ways of the Lord are straight, but the ungodly will stumble in them."

For they are straight, but the ungodly stumble in the ways of the Lord, and so these ways become a stumbling block to people. Those who stumble on the stone of stumbling stumble without distinction: "For they stumbled on the stone of stumbling and took offense."

From the start, the Jews saw the only-begotten Son of God come in the flesh and working divine signs. Because they had not been found worthy of the heavenly knowledge, they said, "Who is this man who speaks blasphemies?" and at another time, "If this man were from God, he would not break the Sabbath." So they did not recognize his Godhead, and took him for nothing more than a man.

Others knew him to be God, but did not recognize his perfect glory. When they heard the profound words spoken about him, and about the dispensation of the flesh carried out for our salvation, they were led astray about his Godhead, for their own reasoning misled them.

For just as the Jews were led astray by [?], so these too are led astray by what they hear. The Jews saw what had been foretold in the prophets, but they were thrown into confusion because they did not recognize it as fulfilled in Christ's coming in the flesh.

These people, in turn, hear the things foretold about his dispensation but understand them in a merely literal way. So they are confused, and they turn what was said to build us up into an argument for their own ruin. They say: He said, "I am going to my God and your God, and to my Father and your Father." "You see that he too is one of the creatures," they dare to say, blaspheming.

28. You see, then, that the dispensation of his coming in the flesh is what misleads them. Let them go back to the beginning and ask about times or seasons, for "his goings forth," it says, "are from the days of eternity." So let us look at what came before these events. The Father says, "Let us make man according to our image and according to likeness." He did not say, "I will make man according to my image."

Be refuted, you whose heart is hardened, as it is written: "But their heart was hardened." Learn that the Son is always with the Father. For the words "let us make" do not point to one person; they are the Father speaking to the Son.

Be refuted too, you who say that the Son is unlike the Father. When he said "according to our image," he did not separate the likeness of the Son from that of the Father, nor did he divide off anything of the Father's identity from the Son. He did not say "according to my image" or "according to your image"; he showed that the Father, the Son and the Spirit are one substance and one Godhead. For he says "according to our image and according to likeness," which means that the Godhead of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit is one, and that man was made according to the image of the one Godhead of Father, Son and Holy Spirit.

Be refuted too, Arius, and listen to the Father saying to the Son "Let us make," calling the Son a fellow creator. I have often heard some people say that the Son made nothing, but that the things that came to be came to be "through him." But if they came to be through him, then he too made them, as has been clearly shown.

For the Word, the master craftsman, is the maker of all things, and the Father works through him. Let them listen to him saying plainly, "My Father is working until now, and I am working"; and in saying this [?] he calls his own Father a fellow creator.

But again, do not let your reasoning deceive you into approaching the Son as a slave and not as the true Master. If he were a slave and not the true Master, how could the one who existed in the form of God have taken the form of a slave when he came? And how could he empty himself if he did not possess fullness? So approach the Son as perfect God, and as the Son who is from the Father.

29. And do not say out of malice: "But the Father said to the Son 'Let us make,' while the Son did not say to the Father 'Let us make.' And the Son does not say 'I am working and my Father is working'; he puts the Father first, as the one who speaks and works."

You say this foolishly, because you want to think of the divine as several first principles. But there is one first principle and one and the same Godhead, and nowhere here does the Son say "my God." I say this not to deny the honor the Son gives to the Father, but to explain how the order of the Godhead stands.
And again: "Adam heard," it says, "God walking in the garden in the evening." Nowhere here does the Son say "my God and your God"; here Scripture speaks of God complete in himself.
And again: "And God spoke to Noah." Nowhere is such an expression found.

"And God appeared," it says, "to Abraham as he sat by the oak of Mamre; and behold, three men. He ran to meet them and bowed down to the ground and said, 'If I have found favor in your sight.'" This shows the one as God, and the other two who accompanied him as his angels.

For about him it also says, "God went up from Abraham." And he himself says to Abraham, "Shall I hide anything from my servant Abraham? The outcry of Sodom and Gomorrah," he says, "has multiplied before me," and so on. Nowhere in those times is "my God and your God" found.

"And the two men went into Sodom," since the one who had gone up above Abraham had parted from the two who went into Sodom to destroy it. About the one who went up, Scripture says, "And the Lord rained fire and brimstone on Sodom and Gomorrah from the Lord." There was no need for the expression "my God and your God."

And Moses says in the Song, "And let all the angels of God worship him." He says "angels of God," just as it says "fire from the Lord," and not simply "angels," to show that the Father and the Son have one kingdom. The angels are not divided among different rulers but belong to God, and they worship the Son, who is God, for an angel does not worship an angel. And nowhere here is there "my God and your God."

30. David says, "The Lord said to my Lord, 'Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies the footstool of your feet.'" "The Lord," he says, "to my Lord." For the dispensation of the flesh did not yet exist, and that is what would make it necessary for him to say "my God and your God."
"Behold, the virgin will conceive and bear a son, and you will call his name Emmanuel, which means 'God with us.'" And there was not yet any need to say "my God and your God."

And: "You, Bethlehem, house of Ephrathah, are not too small to be among the thousands of Judah; for from you one will come forth for me to be ruler in Israel, and his [goings forth] are from the beginning, from the days of eternity." And according to other copies: "And you, Bethlehem, are by no means least among the rulers of Judah; for from you will come a leader who will shepherd my people Israel." And you see that there was not yet any need to say "my God and your God."

But the prophecy of Jeremiah, and likewise of Isaiah, was fulfilled: the Word was born of a virgin and took flesh. As Jeremiah says, "He is also a man, and who will know him?" At that time he took a share in flesh, and without a man's seed he formed for himself that same holy flesh from Mary, the Mother of God, according to the saying "born of a woman." Having shared in what is ours, he says "my God" because of what is ours;

but because his true sonship is eternal and by nature, he says "my Father." Because of his grace toward his disciples he says "your Father," and because of the disciples' own nature in relation to his Godhead and that of his eternal Father, he says "your God."

For he is God of the disciples; he is Father of the Lord by nature, and Father of the disciples by grace. The Father is the Son's God because of the flesh, but his Father because his begetting and true sonship are eternal and beyond comprehension. He truly is his Father, having begotten him in his Godhead outside of time and without beginning.

He had to call him God because of the dispensation he carried out for our sake. He is always with the Father, the Word begotten without beginning, but at the end of days he was born in the flesh from Mary, from that same holy virgin Mary, through the Holy Spirit.
31. So let them understand the depths of God's work, and not turn grace into ingratitude by treating our salvation as a dishonor to the ineffable and incomprehensible nature of God.

"But," they say, "it is written of God, 'He will not hunger or thirst, and his understanding cannot be searched out,' while of the Son it is written that he hungered in the wilderness during the temptation. And it says, 'Our God will not grow weary,' yet the Lord Jesus grew weary on his journey. And 'He who keeps Israel will neither slumber nor sleep,' yet the Lord," they say, "slept in the

boat." How empty are the notions of those who reason this way! When the holy Word came for our sake, he did not only take up our burdens. He also became subject to touch, took flesh, and was found as a man. He was seized by the scribes and [?]: "I gave my back to the whips, and I did not turn my face from the shame of spitting."

He also "wept," as it stands in the Gospel according to Luke in the uncorrected copies. The holy Irenaeus uses this testimony in his work Against Heresies against those who say that Christ only appeared to be human. But orthodox people removed the passage out of fear, because they did not understand its purpose and its great force.
And: "Being in agony he sweated, and his sweat became like clots of blood, and an angel appeared, strengthening him."

Not only this: as a man he also asks, "Where have you laid Lazarus?" and about the woman with the flow of blood, "Who touched me?" and of those looking for him, "Whom are you looking for?" As a man he also asks the disciples, "Who do people say that I, the Son of Man, am?" and again, "How many loaves do you have with you?"

he said. Tired from the journey, he sat down by the well in Samaria. And "the child grew and became strong in spirit," and "Jesus advanced in stature and wisdom." And "before the child knows how to say 'father' or 'mother,' he will take the power of Damascus and the spoils of Samaria,"

he who is Wisdom, who "teaches people knowledge," who "planted the ear in man," who gave articulate speech to the children of men and "made the tongue of stammerers clear." He endured all such things for our sake. He kept to the whole course of the incarnation arranged for us, so that he would not erase the imprint of the truth.

32. We have gathered from the divine Scriptures the countless sayings that the opponents raise against the truth, and we have set them out as if speaking for them. They misunderstand these sayings, and we must not leave them unexplained. So I will set out the meaning of each saying, the force it carries, and the reason it was spoken as if of human feeling.

And we will speak about it again, though we have already said much about "my God and your God," showing how [?] anyone with understanding can recognize from the sequence itself that it was reasonably said.

"For he is a man, and who will know him?" In the same phrase the divine text points to two things, the visible and the invisible. Because of the visible, "my God" is reasonably said; because of the invisible, "my [?]" is said. Neither statement is contradicted by reason.
For if he was a man, how was he not known? And if he was not a man, how was he called a man?
For surely everyone born of human beings is [known] by human beings: by the mother who bore him, by his relatives, by his household, by his neighbors, by those who share his home or his city.

This cannot be fulfilled in a mere man, but it is fulfilled in God the Word, the Son of God. "He is a man" is said because he truly is one, and "who will know him?" because he is God. He shares in human nature, and as God he is unknown to human beings because he is beyond comprehension.
