He is a man truly born of Mary without a man's seed. "The virgin," it says (for the prophet proclaimed the future before its time), "will conceive and bear a son."

If, then, she is a virgin, the conception was not brought about by men. Before this it had been said to Ahaz, "Ask a sign for yourself, in the depth or in the height." But he answered humbly, "I will not ask, and I will not test the Lord my God," declining to ask for a sign.

At once, because he did not ask for a sign, God, who gives great gifts to human beings, grants two. From the height he sent the Word, by his own will and by the Word's own will. From the depth he provided the flesh, by his own good pleasure, together with the Word himself.

For afterward it says, "And they will call his name Emmanuel." He did not say "I will call" but "they will call," for God, who had once been unknown among them, was being revealed to human beings. Yet he does not receive the name as something new, for he did not say "I will call his name Emmanuel," but "they will call."

33. As I have already shown above, the phrase "born of a woman" is there so that, by the words "of a woman," it may be made plain to all that what was born is [flesh], while the Word is eternal. And if "he will not thirst" is a saying about God, while it is said of the Son that he hungered and thirsted, this was arranged because it was necessary for us.
For how could the dispensation be shown to be real if it did not include the ordinary needs that come with becoming human? In this he has given us the answers to all the questions of the heretics.
At once he refuted the notion of the Manichaeans, for when Scripture speaks of eating and drinking, it shows real flesh. He refuted the method of the Lucianists and the argument of Arius.

For Lucian and all the Lucianists deny that the Son of God took a soul. They say he had flesh only, so that they can attach human feelings to God the Word: thirst, hunger, weariness, weeping, grief, distress and everything else recorded of his coming in the flesh. But it would be foolish to attribute these things to the Godhead of the Son of God.
"But," they say, "flesh by itself neither eats nor drinks nor grows weary nor does anything else." I agree that by itself it does not do these things.
But when the Word came, he took on the whole dispensation: flesh, soul and everything that is in a human being. Hunger and weariness, thirst, grief and the rest belonged to the soul and the flesh.

He weeps to refute the error of Mani, showing that he did not wear his body in appearance only but in truth. He thirsts to show that he had not only flesh but also a soul. His Godhead never thirsted. It was in the flesh and in the [soul] that he thirsted and grew weary from the journey, as follows from having flesh and soul.

34. Let the divine Scriptures of the Old and New Testaments persuade them that the Word came with a body and a soul. For at once David speaks about him, and Peter in agreement with David: "You will not abandon my soul to Hades, nor let your holy one see corruption." This is so that we may understand that the Lord's humanity was composite, and come to clear knowledge of it. It establishes that the soul, together with the Godhead, [?] during the three days [?] was laid down with it. It shows the flesh to be holy, and shows that the Godhead together with the soul accomplished the mystery in Hades without being held fast.

Somewhere there is another testimony that says, "free among the dead." "Free" means that Hades had no mastery over him, and that he went down as far as Hades with the soul by his own will. And Peter says, "because it was not possible for him to be held by it," that is, by Hades.

And the Savior himself says, "I have authority to take my soul [and to] lay it down," and "I am the good shepherd, who lays down his soul for the sheep," and "My soul is troubled," he says, "and what shall I say?" (saying "what shall I say?" as if in doubt) "Father, save me from this hour;
but this is why I came to this hour." This shows that his Godhead came to this willingly. And he says "is troubled" so that the reality of his coming in the flesh might not be [?].

For his coming in the flesh was not mere appearance. Think of a great king at war with a weaker enemy. He knows that if his enemy sees him coming in power and great strength, the enemy will refuse to fight, turn and flee, and lay waste many of the lands under his rule. So in his wisdom the king makes excuses, turns his back and runs away, until the enemy takes courage, attacks him as a coward without strength, and pursues him. Then the king suddenly turns with his army and takes the weak opponent wholly into his power. In the same way our Lord did not fear death,

he who, before he came to his passion, told them on the road that the Son of Man was about to be handed over, crucified and raised on the third day. And when Peter said, "Mercy on you, Lord; this will never happen to you," he rebuked him, saying, "Get behind me, Satan, for you are not thinking about the things of God, but the things of men."

So he foretold these things and came for this very purpose. How then could he later pray that the cup might pass, so that he would not drink it? He had spoken about his death before he died, so he could not have prayed for the cup to pass, if only so as not to be taken for a liar.

Rather, by taking on such a role he draws out the adversary. The adversary supposes that the Savior fears death and brings death upon him, and so through the dispensation the Savior brings salvation to those who die.

Even when you hear that the Lord died, know where the suffering of death was fulfilled. For Peter, the chief of the apostles, explains to you the meaning of his death, saying, "put to death in the flesh, but made alive in the spirit." His Godhead took on suffering in the flesh, yet it is impassible, was impassible and remained impassible. Its impassibility was not changed, nor was its eternity altered.

35. The vainglorious may say again: "You cannot persuade us from such words that Christ had a soul. For we have found earlier in the divine Scriptures that Isaiah says, speaking for God the Father about the Only-begotten, 'This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased, whom my soul has loved.'"

What are we to understand about the Father, that he took a soul into himself, or that he has a soul? Who but a fool would think this of the Father? So what do they say? That the saying is obviously meant figuratively.

"If, then," they say, "it is said figuratively of the Father, the same must be understood of the Son as well. So even when he says 'My soul is troubled' and '[I have authority] to give my soul and to take it,' he did not have a soul. It was said figuratively."

Their logic-chopping seems to make a point [?], but the truth stands on its own, supported by many proofs. Each figure of speech is to be understood from the nature of what it describes. In the case of the Father one must not dare to say this, since he never wore flesh. But since the Lucianists, that is, the Arians, acknowledge the flesh, there is no ambiguity.

"But," one of them says, "'The Word became flesh,' and it did not say 'The Word became flesh and soul.'" To their ignorant objection I reply that "God formed man, taking dust from the earth." The word "formed" includes everything, and in the same way "The Word became flesh" includes everything.

By the same reasoning we turn their argument back on them: "Look, it says 'God formed man,' and it did not say he made for him a liver or lungs or a heart or veins or sinews or any of the other parts of the body. Are we to conclude from this that man is a single solid lump, because Scripture did not describe in detail how the whole living being is put together?" Certainly not. Just as Scripture included the whole under one form, so too it is quite clear from the mention of flesh that the Savior took a soul.

36. If, then, he took a soul and a body, as has been shown, then it was not his Godhead that was lessened from the substance of the Father and confined within passions, so that it would thirst, grow weary, hunger and need everything else a human being needs.

Scripture says, "He will not grow weary, and his understanding cannot be searched out," and the Savior is found to be weary. But it does not follow that the Word who came down from above is not of the Father's substance. He did not grow weary above, but in the flesh. The flesh had to grow weary, so that his flesh would not be thought a mere appearance but known to be real.

The other things of this kind, slumbering and sleeping, point to a man, and so does being subject to touch [?]. He took these things on and was found a man. "For we have found," it says, "the Messiah, of whom Moses wrote."

Those who found him [?] through the incomprehensible nature, [?] that is, the nature that took flesh. Because in his incomprehensibility he could not be found, he is seized by scribes, "gave his back to the whips, and did not turn his face from spitting," wept, and endured everything else that is sung about him.

Who could whip or strike or spit on God the Word in heaven, who is so ineffable and incomprehensible? If the impassible Word of God suffered these things, then the suffering was bodily. It was outside his impassibility, and yet again not outside it, because he was pleased to accept it.

Although he did not suffer, the suffering is counted as his. A stain on a garment does not reach the body of the wearer, yet the stain is attributed to the wearer. In the same way God suffered in the flesh, while his Godhead suffered nothing. The suffering of the flesh, which the Godhead wore, was counted as the Godhead's, so that our salvation might come about in the Godhead.
37. I also recall the passage in the Gospel according to Luke, and I do not want to leave it unexplained. It is written: "Being in agony he sweated, and his sweat became like clots of blood.

And an angel of the Lord appeared, strengthening him." As we usually say, the deeper and more essential sayings are the ones that people who do not grasp their meaning use to overturn themselves by their wickedness [?], instead of drawing good from them. Yet nothing could be more fitting than this passage.

By saying "he was in agony," it shows that the Lord's man was a real man. And to show that he was truly a man and that the agony did not come from the Godhead, it says, "He sweated, and his sweat became like clots of blood." This is a bodily phenomenon, not a spiritual one.

"And an angel of the Lord appeared, strengthening him." This does not mean that he who is greater than the angels needed an angel's strength. He is the one "to whom every knee bows, in heaven and on earth and under the earth." He is forever God the Word, forever with the Father and begotten from him. Rather, it happened to fulfil what is in the great Song of Moses, sung in the wilderness, where he said, "Let all the sons of God worship him, and let the angels of God strengthen him."

"Let them strengthen him" does not mean that they supply him with strength. Their doxology had the power to glorify God in these terms: the angels above, and the spiritual living creatures, at once cry out, "Yours is the power, yours is the might, yours is the strength." In this way the passage shows what it means to worship and to strengthen, namely to ascribe to him the might that belongs to strength. So too the angel appeared before the disciples worshipping his own Master.

The angel was not unaware of how surpassing his loving dispensation was. He marvelled at the great work of meekness accomplished in him, which defeated the devil, crushed the sting of death, triumphed over the principalities and powers, and shattered sin.

Because this was so surpassingly wonderful, the angel worshipped and said in his doxology: "Yours is the strength, Master. You have prevailed against death and against Hades and against the devil, to crush his sting and cast it out of humanity."

38. Again, he may say in human fashion, "Where have you laid Lazarus?" Or he may say about the woman with the flow of blood, "Who touched me?" Or there are sayings like "Whom do you seek?", "Who do people say that I, the Son of Man, am?", "The child grew and became strong," "He advanced in stature and wisdom," and "Before the child knows how to call father or mother." Do you not see from the subject matter itself how surpassing his knowledge was, and that these accounts come from the flesh and the humanity?

In the Old Testament, some things are spoken in the person of God the Father that come down to the human level in order to persuade people. They seem to involve ignorance, yet nothing was unknown to God. When the Word came, he fulfilled these things, so as to fulfil the saying, "My Father is working until now, and I am working." "Where have you laid Lazarus?"

he asked when he was near the place. But before he came to the place, without hearing it from anyone, he said to his disciples, "Our friend Lazarus has fallen asleep." So he knew that Lazarus had died while he was many days' journey from the place. Was he then ignorant when he was actually there?
Not at all. Since no one yet fully believed in him, he wanted to show why he did all these things: to display the great love for humanity in his care for us.

Those women should not have said, "It is the fourth day; he already stinks," or gone off to show him the place. They should have said, "You know all things, and if you will it, he will live." That is why he wept at people's hardness of heart. So he did not ask out of ignorance. He was testing and reproving them, and showing his love for humankind.

And he says, "Who touched me?" It was not that he did not know who touched him. He did not want to announce the miracle himself. He wanted the woman to hear, come forward and tell of the grace done to her, and after confessing it to hear, "Your faith has saved you." In this way he would encourage others too to believe and be healed.

He says, "Who do people say that I, the Son of Man, am?" In the same way, in the Old Testament he says in the person of the Father, "Adam, where are you?" Yet he knew where Adam was. That is why he reproves him afterwards, saying, "You have eaten from the tree."

And he asked Cain, "Where is Abel your brother?" He did not ask out of ignorance, for he says, "Cursed are you on the earth, which opened its mouth to receive your brother's blood from your hand. For see, his blood cries out to me." So the one who says that the blood cries out was not ignorant. He asked in order to give Cain room for repentance and a chance to defend himself.

39. But they turn again to their ignorant quarrelling and say that these Old Testament utterances belong to the Son himself. Their trick is refuted at once. The one who said to Moses, "What is this in your hand?" is the same one who said, "I am He who is."

And when the Lord explains the resurrection to the Sadducees, he says: "That the dead are raised, God said: I am the God of Abraham and the God of Isaac and the God of Jacob. So he is the God of the living and not of the dead."
Again, it can be shown that many things in the Old Testament were said in the person of the Father. Many were also said in the person of the Son, and others again in the person of the Holy Spirit.
And it was the Son of God, who came from above with the two angels, who said to Abraham, "Where is Sarah your wife?" If he had not known where she was, he would not have said "Sarah."

[?] "So Sarah laughed, being inside." He wants to point to her modesty as a pattern for women who wish to be truly devout. When they receive guests, they should serve with their own labour, but out of modesty they should not show their faces to the men.

That blessed woman certainly prepared everything. Having prepared it, she did not appear before the angels, and so she gave a pattern of modesty to the generations that followed. And to show who it was that was present, the one who was a guest for that hour called the woman by name [?]. [?] This showed that neither her name nor the human frame nor human thought escaped him.

He says, "Who do people say that I, the Son of Man, am?" He uses the title "Son of Man" himself, confessing it, so that they would not think he was asking about the invisible one. They say Elijah, Jeremiah and John. "But who do you say that I am?" Peter says, "You are the Christ, the Son of the living God," and he is at once pronounced blessed.

He did not ask out of ignorance. He wanted to show that the teaching which proclaims to the church that the Son is true God comes from the Father, and so he let Peter say what he had been taught by the Father.

40. Do not be surprised if he says, "Through me they come to the Father," and do not take this to mean that he is of a different essence from the Father. He himself also teaches, "No one comes to me unless the Father draws him." Just as the Father sends people to the Son, so the Son brings them to the Father, to show that the Godhead is one and the same.

Then there is "he advanced," "he advanced also in wisdom." If he is the Wisdom of God, he does not lack wisdom. Rather, he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, but the fullness was not [?] diminished. [?] The point is to show that he was emptied out from heaven into humanity, that is, into the workshop of Mary.

Scripture says, "Your name is ointment emptied out." It did not say "poured out" but "emptied out": from heaven to earth, so that from [?] into Mary. And from Mary, having become flesh, he is conceived. He is born in Bethlehem. From Bethlehem he moves to Nazareth, from Nazareth to Capernaum, from Capernaum to Jerusalem. He goes to the sea, when he walks on the water, and to the region of Tyre, to Nain, to Judea and Jericho, and to Bethphage and Bethany. He goes to Jerusalem, to the temple, to the Mount of Olives and Gethsemane, to the house of Caiaphas, to the praetorium and to Herod. He goes to the place called Golgotha, to the tomb and down to Hades, back to earth after the resurrection, and up to the heavens.
Ointment emptied from one vessel into another makes all the vessels fragrant. In the same way, the coming of Christ from heaven sanctified the whole earth, that is, those who receive him in truth.

He is the mountain, as in Daniel [?], and a great mountain. He is "a stone cut out without hands" [?], which hints at his birth without a man's seed. The greater is found small again. Then the stone takes back its greatness and becomes a great mountain once more, a mountain not confined to one place but filling the whole inhabited world.
This is the one who is Wisdom [?] and became man. He extended his power through the world in order to fill the world with grace, and so "he advanced in stature and wisdom."

He is the Wisdom of the Father. He "teaches human beings" to speak, he formed the tongue for them, and he "planted the ear" in those who hear. How then could he not know how to call father or mother? [?] "He will take the power of Damascus and the spoils of Samaria," and so on?

But suppose he had shown himself speaking as soon as he was born from the womb, and had talked clearly as a newborn. Then his conception in the flesh would have been thought an illusion and not real [?], or rather a mere appearance. That is exactly why he submits to the smallness of infancy: so as not to destroy the truth of the natural sequence.

41. Again they hunt for [?] other empty notions, weave them into the divine words and understand them perversely. They say: How then is it written, "Receive the high priest of our confession, who was faithful to him who made him"? And "Let all the house of Israel know that God has made this Jesus, whom you crucified, both Lord and Christ"?

I am greatly amazed that people who handle the sequence of these passages do not know the meaning they express. The words "Receive the high priest, who was faithful to him who made him" are not said about the Godhead.
For God came [?], and the divine Scriptures make everything clear to us. Nothing in them is crooked or twisted. Everything is plain to those who understand and straight to those who find knowledge.

For it says, "Receive instruction and not silver." Unless someone receives instruction from God, that is, the faith of the truth, everything is crooked and perverse to him. But to those who understand rightly and find knowledge, everything is straight and blameless.
To refute them, the apostle says: "Every high priest taken from among men is appointed on behalf of men in matters relating to God, to offer gifts and sacrifices."

That is why the Only-begotten himself, since he came to become high priest on behalf of men, took flesh from us. He who came from us became an offering for us to his own Father, God, so that he might "call" the disciples "brothers." Where, then, is "having become" fulfilled? Nowhere else but in the high priest. For it says, "Receive the high priest, who was faithful to him who made him."

Let me use a fuller illustration. Suppose someone asks a king about his own son and boldly says to him, "Who is this?" He hears the father's rightful acknowledgment, "He is my son," and asks again, "Your son by nature?" When the king says yes, the questioner goes on, "What then did you make him?" The king would surely say, "I made him king." By naming the rank, did he deny that the son was his true-born child?
When he states the second thing, has he wiped out the first? Not at all. In the same way, God the Father begot the Son without beginning, and "he made him high priest" is fulfilled in the flesh.

42. But, they say, it is written, "The Lord created me as the beginning of his ways for his works." First of all, these conceited people do not know the name of the book. The book is called the Proverbs of Solomon. And whatever is said in proverbs does not mean the same as the literal force of the words.
Look: our Lord Jesus Christ spoke in parables, and we see that the parables do not correspond literally to the matter in hand.

For he says, "The kingdom of heaven is like a grain of mustard seed." If we try to understand the parable in part, by our own reasoning, the kingdom of heaven is clearly a place of great spaciousness.

If one must speak of a place at all, this is the kingdom in which the king is God the Father, and God the Word, the Son of God, and the Holy Spirit of God, along with angels and archangels, the spiritual hosts, Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and all the righteous. How could so many be contained in a mustard seed? No, the figurative expression is spoken in riddles. So what is said in proverbs is not the same as the literal meaning.

The kingdom is also compared to a woman who had ten drachmas, lost one, lit a lamp and found it; to a net cast into the sea; and to seed sown on the [?]. All these are said in riddles and do not mean the same as their literal force.
And we do not really know whether Solomon, the writer of proverbs, said this about the Son of God. For there is wisdom and there is wisdom.

The apostle can say, "The world did not know God through the wisdom of God," and "God made foolish the wisdom of the world," and again, "not in fleshly wisdom but in the power of God." Solomon too can speak of wisdom when he says, "I fell in love with her beauty and took her as my bride." Job also knows of wisdom and says, "But where is wisdom found? And where is the place of understanding?" We also find "The wisdom of the poor man is despised," and "He is the corrector of wisdom," and "The Only-begotten is the Wisdom of the Father."
43. What do we say, then? The Father is wise. If, as they think, the Son did not come forth from him, though he is Word and God and Wisdom, then the Father lacks wisdom in himself.

How then can it say, "to the only wise, invisible God" [?], and how are all these things incomprehensible and boundless for human beings? God gave wisdom to Solomon and filled Bezalel with wisdom, and "wise men hide shame."
There is much to say about wisdom. But that Wisdom of the Father is unique in kind and has no other wisdom to compare with it.

Still, even if the passage that is sung was about that Wisdom, I neither accept nor reject it, but leave the knowledge to God. I see that the statements are strained and contradict one another. For it says, "He created me as the beginning of his ways for his works; before the age he founded me; before all the hills he begets me."
How then can what is begotten be founded? And how can what is created be begotten? If it is created, it is not truly begotten.
What we beget we do not create, and what we create we do not beget. Yet we are created, and what we beget is created. But in God, who is uncreated, the offspring is not created.
If he begot, he did not create. And if he begot again after creating, how could what was first created be begotten later?
So if these words are about him, they are fulfilled in the dispensation of the incarnation. That is why the passage speaks first of the nearer things and tells of the more ancient things afterwards.

Wishing to persuade human beings, who are nearest, it begins with the flesh. (The beginning of the ways of the righteousness of the gospel is that the Word became flesh for us in Mary, and a soul was founded in her flesh.) It does so in order to show the higher things afterwards.

And we say that he came from the Father's bosom, from heaven to earth, since he came to us later, once he had accomplished the whole dispensation. So the Word is not created (God forbid!), and divine Scripture has produced nothing crooked for us at all.

44. Moreover, the expression is not rendered this way by its natural sense or by the translators. Aquila says, "The Lord acquired me," since the Hebrew reads "Adonai qanani," which means what we have said. We too, in everyday speech, say of people who beget that they have "acquired children."

Even so, he did not settle the meaning of the translation. "Adonai qanani" can also be translated "The Lord nested me." That is why Peter speaks clearly when he says, "this Jesus, whom you crucified." He did not say God the Word from above, but "this Jesus" [?]: the flesh conceived together with the Word from above in Mary's womb. He calls it "this" because of the Lord's man from Mary.

In this the † "created" is also fulfilled. As Peter says, "put to death in the flesh, but made alive in the spirit," and again, "Since Christ therefore suffered for us in the flesh." And again, as Paul says, "from whom is Christ according to the flesh."

The Saviour himself said in the Gospel, "But now you seek to kill me, a man who has told you the truth that I heard from the Father." He said this to show that the suffering came from his humanity and [?] below, but that he is the natural Son of the Father from above.

Paul the holy apostle also agrees with this when he says, "There is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus," "who did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant."

You see that he declared him a man, but not a mere man. He is called "mediator between God and men" because he mediates for both sides. Toward his Father he is God by nature, genuinely begotten. Toward human beings he is a natural, genuine man, born of Mary without a man's seed. This is how he is mediator between God and men: he is God and has become man, without being changed in nature, and in each respect he mediates toward both.

45. But again, in their ignorance, they say: "You see that 'he did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped.'" These quarrelsome people do not even know the wording. He did not say, "He did not wish to become equal to God by seizing it." He said, "He did not count being equal with God a thing to be grasped," that is, being God by nature, because that is what he was.

If he was not equal to God, how could he take the form of a servant? The passage indicated something new, and from this it showed in wonder how surpassing [?] it was: although he was equal to God, he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant. He did not do this to enslave what was free, but so that in the form he took he might set free the servants who obey.

The Jews also testify that he was not ashamed to call himself equal to God and did not hesitate, but [?] showed it all the more boldly [?] by saying, "If I do not say it, I shall be a liar like you." That is why they say to him, "We are not killing you for a good work, but because you, being a man, make yourself equal to God."

But they say: "We must confess the figurative [?] about him." Scripture has indeed said many figurative things about him, and we must not deny what was said about him in riddles. He has been called a door, and a stone, and a pillar, a cloud, a lion, a sheep, a lamp, a torch, the sun, an angel, a worm, a rock, a cornerstone, the way, a bull, a calf, and the like.

Clearly we do not deny what was fulfilled in him through riddles. But we know why these things were written. He is the way because through him we walk to the kingdom, to him and to the Father. He is the door because through him we enter. He is a pillar because he is the foundation of our faith. He is a rock because he cannot be moved. He is a stone because he has been laid as a foundation. He is the sun of righteousness because he has shone on our darkened minds.

46. Then they say that if it is written of him that he is a creature, we must also confess "creature." Well, I too have listed some of the uses of the riddles about him that have been fulfilled for us.

So let them tell us what purpose is served by calling him a creature. He is rightly called a door, figuratively, so that he may be our entrance and our benefit. He is called the way, so that walking through him we may not go astray. But a creature:

what does that do for us? How does it benefit us? "Yes," says the conceited man, quarrelling, "if you do not call him a creature, you attribute passion to the Father. Everyone who begets is subject to passion: he either contracts, or expands, or is spread out, or flows away, or swells, or undergoes something of that kind."

Alas for such a mind, so wicked and so far from the truth! Who will think such things about God? What kind of notion would dare to suggest them? Clearly no one, not even any of the demons, would think anything of the sort.
Anyone who confesses the Father believes that he truly begot the Son. [?] For the divine does not consist of bulk, nor is it a pregnant body, that it should undergo the things just mentioned.

"For God is spirit," and spirit does not undergo flowing, cutting, contraction, diminution, spreading, or anything of the kind. So, since the Father is spirit, he begot the Son, God the Word, spiritually, timelessly, incomprehensibly and without beginning.

47. To persuade people who think this way, let us speak without claiming that the cases are alike, but turning back their bad defence by means of a comparable example. Take a created thing that falls infinitely short of its Master, ten thousand times over.

Many people in the desert who need fire fill a glass vessel with water and bring material that catches fire easily, made of linen or tow. They stand facing the sun, and as the glass casts the sun's glare onto the material beneath, fire is at once taken from the sun and kindles. Has the sun been cut by sharing its substance? Has it failed? Has it been diminished? No, they say.

If, then, the sun was not diminished, though it is a creature, how much more is this true of God, who is infinite, incomprehensible and undefiled! Being spirit, he begot from himself God the Word, who is ineffable, incomprehensible and incorruptible, and he begot him in incorruption. He did so not through passion, not by cutting, not by any loss, but as the perfect begetting the perfect in perfection.
The nature of fire lights many lamps from one, and the first lamp is not diminished. And again, the same substance can be made up of many separate parts, I mean lamps or torches.
But the divine is not like that, God forbid! The Word did not come back and merge with the Father. The Father is Father, the Son is Son, and the Holy Spirit is Holy Spirit.

48. The Manichaeans' claim is foolish. They say that in the [?] of Mani the souls, which came from the column of light, are one body, and that when they are released from their bodies they are formed again into the one substance, as though gathered into the one column, according to [?] their fabrication.

But the Gospel did not show it to be so. He broke five loaves and fed five thousand, and he did not let the leftovers go. "Gather them up," he says, "and leave none of the fragments," and they gathered twelve baskets.

They gathered them together into the containers, but he did not join the fragments back into loaves as they had been. They gathered up the whole quantity, but as many fragments; what he showed was one gathering of baskets.

We have not allegorized this, or the example of the sun given earlier, as a speculative theory. We do not say that the loaves are souls, or the fragments either, God forbid. Nor do we make God equal to the sun he created, or the Only-begotten equal to the radiance the sun sends into the tow.

In the same way, souls that are born are not joined into one fused mass, God forbid. They go into the dwelling places of God, of which it is written, "There are many dwelling places with the Father." They do not become one heap, but each is counted individually.

Nor, when we say that God has begotten his only-begotten Son, do we ascribe passion to him, as their wicked blasphemy claims. "For everyone who begets labors under passion, and so one must call him neither a creature nor an offspring," according to their argument, "lest we present God as toiling or suffering." Where, then, did we find the Son, or why does he bear the name of Son?

These are human syllogisms that start from earthly ways of thinking. It is unlawful to attribute our human passions to God, for God says plainly, "My thoughts are not like your thoughts," and again, "God is not as a human being."

49. So let them stop their blasphemy and learn from the Father, who says, "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased." Again, speaking of things still to come, he says, "For you are my beloved Son, whom I have chosen," and then in the Song, "chosen out of ten thousands." Let them tell us, then, what the choosing was made from.
For the babblers think that because he says "I have chosen," he is called Son by grace and not by nature. Let them show who is like him, so that God could have tested them all and then chosen him.

If he is the only-begotten Son, there is no one equal or comparable to him, for he is "like the Son among the sons of God." Those others he knows as sons by grace, but no one can be made equal to him, because he is Son by nature.
It is clear what he was "chosen out" of and where the choosing lies. There were many ten thousands on the earth, and Mary alone "found favor," and in her he chose the holy flesh.

That is why he said "I am well pleased." David also speaks in the person of the apostles, who believed in the Lord and joyfully showed his grace to the nations: "He has subjected peoples to us and nations under our feet; he has chosen for us his inheritance, the beauty of Jacob, which he loved." That is, the purest part of his beauty,

the beauty of all of Jacob: the flesh chosen from Mary through the Holy Spirit. [?] The Father showed John the Baptist from above what had come about through the dispensation of the flesh. For the Father was well pleased in Christ's coming in the flesh, while the Godhead possesses its nature infinitely [?].
50. The apostle also calls him "Son of love": "who rescued us," he says, "from the power of darkness and transferred us into the kingdom of the Son of his love."

Here too the babblers do not understand the expression, and they say that the Son belongs to God by advancing in love. The ignorant do not know the counterpart to this statement, for in another place the apostle says, "God loved us in Christ."

The Only-begotten is truly the beloved Son. The Father is love and the Son is love, since he is love from love. He is Son of love, then, both because of us and because of himself, for in him God loved us and gave up his only-begotten Son for us. So God neither toils when he works nor suffers when he begets.

Let them not heap blasphemies on themselves for nothing. If the Son is created, then by their own argument he is not to be worshiped. It is foolish to worship a creature and to set aside the first commandment, which says, "Hear, O Israel: the Lord your God is one Lord."

So the holy Word is not created, because he is worshiped. The disciples worshiped him, and the angels in heaven worship him. For it says, "Let all the angels of God worship him," and "I will worship you, O Lord, my strength."

There is one point that is explicit, brief and beyond dispute, which no one can contradict. If those who are hostile to the Son of God have any testimony, let them show where, in the Old or the New Testament, the Father said, "I created a Son for myself," or where the Son said, "The Father created me." There are four Gospels, with one thousand one hundred and sixty-two chapters. From beginning to end the Son spoke, and the Father spoke to him, and nowhere did the Son say, "My Father created me," nor did the Father say, "I created a Son for myself" or "I created my Son."

51. But the contentious and vainglorious man says, "What, then, do you say about the body?" Clearly, that it was taken from Mary. "And what is Mary?" he says. "Uncreated or created?" Created, clearly; we say so ourselves, since she was born of a man and a woman. "Then what do you say about what came from Mary? Do you worship the Savior in the body, or not?" How could I not worship him? If I do not worship him, I do not have life. "There you are, then: you worship a creature, the body." Those who say such things are badly deranged.

A king clothed in purple is worshiped by everyone. Is it the purple that is worshiped, or the king? Plainly the king. Yet the purple he is wearing is worshiped along with him. But when the king takes it off and lays it aside, the purple is no longer worshiped.

A king also often sits in a temple on his own throne, and those who worship him worship the king in his own temple and on the throne. But once the king has risen, no one worships either the temple or the throne. And no one, even a madman, who wishes to worship the king in his temple says to him, "Come out of your temple so that I may worship you."

In the same way no one should say to the Only-begotten, "Lay aside the body so that I may worship you." Rather, one worships the Only-begotten together with the body, the uncreated one together with the holy temple that he took when he came.

No one says to the king, "Get up from your throne so that I may worship you apart from the throne"; one worships the king together with the throne. So too Christ is worshiped together with the body that was buried and raised.

52. "But what, then, do you say?" they ask. "Did the Father beget the Son willingly or unwillingly? For you say that the Word always existed and that there was no time before the Word." Yet even the Arians themselves, to deceive certain people, say that the Son of God was begotten timelessly. They do not want to call him eternal, though, and they say, "There was once when he was not." They suppose that "once" does not mean time.

But if you examine the expression, you refute the ignorant. Taken literally, "once" signifies time. When they say it does not mean time, their bad faith lands their thinking in absurdity. They use words with dissimulation, while in their thoughts they are fiercely at war against the Son of God, shamelessly holding him to be wholly foreign to the Father's Godhead. "So did he beget willingly or unwillingly?"

If we say unwillingly, we put the divine under necessity. If we say willingly, we grant that the will existed before the Word. Even if it were an instant, the twinkling of an eye, or the smallest fraction of an hour, that fraction signifies time before the Word, and again we fall in with their argument. And if we say he begot not willingly, then the divine was driven by a necessity of nature and not by the freedom of its will.

But none of this applies to God, as you suppose, you vainglorious man, for such things do not exist with God. He begot neither willingly nor unwillingly, but by the transcendence of his nature. The divine nature surpasses deliberation; it does not fall under time and it is not driven by necessity.

With us nothing is ready at hand, because once we did not exist. First we deliberate about something, then we do what we do; and if we have not deliberated, what we have not yet done does not exist. But with God all things are perfect and smooth, and all things are complete in him. He begot neither willingly nor unwillingly the one who is properly his own, the holy Word and God begotten of him; he begot him in his transcendent and ineffable nature.

53. I am filled with the greatest wonder, children of the faith and of the Church, at how the contentious have twisted what is literal into allegory, while they mistakenly take what is said figuratively as literal. Being begotten belongs to him by nature, yet they say he is not begotten like one of the things that are begotten. Being created is foreign to his Godhead, and even if it was once said by way of allegory, they call that the literal truth and erase what really is true.

For Isaiah says, "I saw the Lord of hosts"; Scripture says, "The Lord appeared to Moses," "The Lord appeared to Abraham," and "Daniel saw a vision, the Ancient of Days," and so on; and the Lord appeared to Ezekiel, and he said, "I saw the likeness of God." Yet they say these things did not happen, falsely accusing the prophets,

supposedly on the basis of the Gospel text where the Savior said in his teaching, "No one has ever seen God." And they say, "If the Only-begotten said that no one has seen him, and the prophets say they have seen him, then either the Only-begotten or the prophets must be lying."

By the reasoning of those who talk like this, and of the Manichaeans, what is in the prophets will be false. But if the prophets do not lie but speak the truth, as the Savior's word says, "I who speak in the prophets, here I am," then the matter needs to be understood and calls for allegory.

This is often borne out in the following way. We see the sea in part from a mountain or a plain, and we speak the truth in saying so. Yet if someone says he has not seen it, he is not lying but speaking the truth, for he does not know where its depth or its length lies; he does not know its mass or its extent.

We also look at the sky through some opening, but we do not know its full expanse. If someone says, "I saw it," he saw it; and if another says, "I did not see it," he did not see it. We truly saw it as far as we can take it in, but we did not see it as it is.
So too the prophets were counted worthy to see as though through an opening, through the narrow passage of their own body, and in [?]

they saw, but not as the infinity of the vision really is. In this way the divine Scriptures are fulfilled in harmony with one another: the prophets say they have seen (for they truly saw), and the Savior says, "No one has ever beheld God" (for they did not see him as he is). But he himself saw the nature invisibly, and to one who could not see he gave a power of grace to see the power of the vision.

54. But do not put on a show again and say, "The prophets saw, not with their eyes but with the mind, all but understanding and not [?]." This is exactly why Isaiah says, "Woe is me, for I am pierced to the heart! For I am a man with unclean lips, and I live among a people with unclean lips, and I have seen the Lord of hosts." He did not say "I saw with my mind," but "with my eyes." So they saw and did not see. They saw as far as they were able, and they saw in truth, but they did not see as the infinity of his incomprehensibility really is.
In the same way many people allegorize paradise too, just as Origen, that God-accursed man, chose to introduce fantasy rather than truth into life. He says, "There is no paradise on earth,"

supposedly on the basis of what the holy apostle said: "I know a man who fourteen years ago, whether in the body I do not know, or out of the body I do not know, God knows, was caught up to the third heaven." But do not misread this and say that "third" means the third part of the air. In saying "to the [third] heaven" he is not speaking of a third part but of three in number.
And he says, "I know such a man, who was caught up into paradise and heard words that no human being is permitted to speak."

Glory to God Almighty, who makes things clear in every way and speaks with precision, so that the true [?] may not be led astray. He did not join heaven and paradise in one brief phrase. He says, "I know a man caught up to the third heaven," and again, "caught up into paradise." The phrase with the article marks off a separate subject and indicates a move to another place.

Suppose someone has a mountain and a plain, with the plain surrounding the mountain, and he wants to reach the far side of the mountain within that same plain. If he wants to make the journey through the plain to the place beyond the mountain where he wishes to go, he can do so. If instead he wants first to climb the mountain and then come down from the mountain to the part of the plain beyond it, he can do that too.

Understand what the apostle said in this way: first he went up into heaven, and then he went down into paradise, as it is said, "My beloved went down into his garden." [?] And the Savior says, "Today you will be with me in paradise."
55. But if paradise is not on earth, and what is written in Genesis is not true but allegory, then nothing in the whole sequence is true and everything becomes allegory.

"In the beginning," it says, "God made the heaven and the [earth]." These are not allegories but visible things. It also speaks of the firmament and the sea, shoots and trees and plants, grass, animals, fish and birds: all the things that are seen, and that truly came to be. And he made the human being, who truly exists.
He placed this man whom he had formed in paradise, having made this same man after the image, after the image of God.
Do not pry into God's gifts, which were given to humankind by grace. We do not deny that all human beings are after the image of God.
But we do not pry into how they are after the image. We do not take the image to mean the formed body, or the soul, or the mind, or virtue, for there are many reasons that prevent me from saying so.

Yet neither do we say that the body or the soul is not after the image. It is for believers to acknowledge Scripture, not for unbelievers; it is unbelievers who "set aside the grace." So being after the image is present in human beings, but God himself knows how.

If you say that he made man after the image and you think this means the body, then since God is invisible, incomprehensible and beyond conception, how will what is visible, comprehensible and subject to touch be an image of the invisible and incomprehensible?

And if you say the body is not after the image, Scripture says, "He took dust from the earth and formed the man." It calls what is made of earth "man," and it calls the soul "man" too, for it says, "He breathed into his face the breath of life, and the man became a living soul."

We hold that both the soul and the body are created. How is the soul created? Scripture says "he breathed"; and we neither say that the soul is a part of God nor that it is foreign to the breathing-in. How this is to be understood in detail is known to God alone.

56. But we believe God, who speaks truly in all things, without prying and without guile. And if you say that the soul is what is after the image, [?] for the apostle says, "The word of God is living and active, sharper than any two-edged sword, piercing even to the dividing of soul."

If, then, the soul has divisions, and God is indivisible, how can the soul be what is after the image? The soul does not know the future, but God knows everything. And we see what is in front of the body but do not know what is behind it. Yet if you say that it is not the soul, he has certainly called the soul "man" as well, and a human being is both soul and body.

But you might say that the mind is what is after the image. Scripture says, "I see another law at war in my members, taking me captive in my mind to the law of sin that is in my members." How then can what is taken captive be after the image? [?] "I will sing with the mind, I will sing with the spirit."

If you say that virtue is what is after the image, I will reply: tell me about Adam. What virtue did he practice before he was formed? He did not exist in the beginning, yet he was formed after the image from the beginning. And if you say it is not virtue, you are not speaking rightly either. For what is more fitting to be after the image than virtue? But man was formed after the image before there was any virtue. Adam had not yet lived a life of virtue, [?] since clearly he had not even been created.

And if you say that baptism is what is after the image, then were the righteous who did not receive baptism not after the image? The type began with Moses and the sea, the grace was opened with John, and the gift was perfected in Christ.

57. All, then, have what is after the image, but not by nature. Human beings do not have it as equals of God. God is incomprehensible and beyond conception; he is spirit, spirit beyond all spirit, and light beyond all light.
But we do not deprive man of what God himself has given, for he who by grace gave man what is after the image is truthful. And this can be understood from similar cases.

We see that the Savior took into his hands, as the Gospel has it, when he was reclining at supper, he took such-and-such, and after giving thanks he said, "This is my such-and-such." And he gave it to his disciples and said, "This is my such-and-such."
And we see that it is not equal or similar, either to the incarnate image, or to the invisible Godhead, or to the features of his limbs. For it is round in shape [?] and without sensation.

[?] as regards its power, and by grace he chose to say, "This is my such-and-such," and no one disbelieves his word. Whoever does not believe that he is truthful in what he said falls away from grace and salvation.

When we hear, let us also believe. We believe that it is his [?]; and we know that our Lord is wholly sensation, wholly perceptive, wholly God, wholly moving, wholly active, wholly light, wholly Word, incomprehensible, yet he has given us this by grace.

58. This Adam, then, was placed in paradise and ate from the tree. And paradise, Scripture says, is "in Eden, toward the east." "A spring went up out of Eden," it says. It did not say "came down," so that we should not think Eden is in heaven; if it were in heaven, it would have said that a spring "comes down" from above. It also says, "A river goes out of Eden," and it did not say "comes down."

This river "divides into four heads. The name of the first is Pishon," and we see the Pishon before our eyes. The Pishon is the river that the Indians and Ethiopians call the Ganges, while the Greeks call it the Indus. "For it encircles the whole land of Havilah," that is, lesser and greater Ethiopia, the regions of the Havilaeans. It crosses greater Ethiopia, turns toward the south, and sinks into the great Ocean on the near side of Gadeira.

The second river is "Gihon." We see this river as something perceptible, not an allegory. It is the river that comes down through Ethiopia, crosses lesser Ethiopia, the lands of the Anubites, the Blemmyes and the Axumites, floods the regions of the Thebaid and Egypt, and empties into this sea of ours. If anyone disbelieves this, let him listen to Jeremiah, who says, "What have you to do with the land of Egypt, to drink the muddy water of Gihon?"

"The third river," it says, "is the Tigris, which flows opposite the Assyrians." It cuts through the regions of the East, sinks under the earth, rises from Armenia between the Carduaeans and the Armenians, springs up again, and cuts through into the land of the Assyrians.

The fourth river, the Euphrates, likewise sinks under the earth in the same way, comes up from Armenia, and so floods Persia. If, then, there is no perceptible paradise, there is no spring; if there is no spring, there is no river; if there is no river, there are no four heads; if there is no Pishon, there is no Gihon and no Tigris; if there is no Tigris, there is no Euphrates;

if there is no Euphrates, there is no fig tree and there are no leaves, there is no Adam, there is no eating [?], there is no Eve; if there is no Eve, he did not eat from the tree; if he did not eat from the tree, there is no Adam;

and if there is no Adam, there are no human beings. Truth becomes a myth from then on, and everything is turned into allegory. But Adam does exist. We come from him; we are all his race by succession, and we see him through the multitude of his descendants.

59. For Adam begets Seth according to his own form and according to his own image. So that no one would think that the one who was fashioned and those who were begotten were different beings, Scripture says, "according to his form and according to his image." Seth begets Enosh, Enosh Kenan, Kenan Mahalalel, Mahalalel Jared, and Jared Enoch, Enoch Methuselah, Methuselah Lamech, Lamech Noah. Then the flood came, not as an allegory but in reality, and every soul perished, but "eight souls" of human beings remained.

And if you hear "souls," do not suppose that they had no bodies. The whole human being is named from one of its parts. "Jacob went down into Egypt," Scripture says, "with seventy-five souls." This does not mean that souls went along without bodies. They went with their bodies, so Scripture has named the whole human being. And Luke, who wrote the Acts of the Apostles, says, "We were in the ship, about eighty souls."

Ordinary usage, too, is in the habit of calling slaves "bodies." "He is master of a hundred bodies," people say, yet those slaves have souls as well. But since human mastery rules over bodies and not over souls, people have reasonably called slaves "bodies," although they have souls, to indicate that it is their bodies that are put to use.

Noah came out of the ark, having begotten Shem, Ham and Japheth. Shem begets Arphaxad, Arphaxad begets Cainan, Cainan Shelah, Shelah Eber, Eber Peleg, Peleg Reu, Reu Serug, Serug Nahor, Nahor Terah, Terah Abraham, Abraham Isaac, Isaac Jacob, Jacob Judah, Judah Perez, Perez Hezron, Hezron Aram, Aram Amminadab, Amminadab Nahshon, Nahshon Salmon, Salmon Boaz, Boaz Obed by Ruth, Obed Jesse, Jesse David the king, David Solomon by the wife of Uriah, Solomon Rehoboam, Rehoboam Abijah, Abijah Asaph, Asaph Jehoshaphat, Jehoshaphat Joram, Joram Ahaziah, Ahaziah Joash, Joash Amaziah, Amaziah Uzziah, who was also called Azariah, Uzziah Jotham, Jotham Ahaz, Ahaz Hezekiah, Hezekiah Manasseh, Manasseh Amos, Amos Josiah, Josiah Jechoniah, Jechoniah in turn Shealtiel, Shealtiel Zerubbabel, Zerubbabel Abiud, Abiud Eliakim, Eliakim Azor, Azor Zadok, Zadok Achim, Achim Eliud, Eliud Eleazar, Eleazar Matthias, Matthias Jacob, Jacob Joseph.

60. Joseph was an old man and a widower. He had earlier taken a first wife and had by her four sons and two daughters. The sons were James, who is called the brother of the Lord because he was brought up together with him, Simon, Judas and Joses. The daughters were † Anna and Salome.

This Joseph, old and a widower, received the holy Virgin Mary by lot. This happened by necessity: in each tribe lots were cast among widowers and unmarried men for the virgins who came from the temple, because firstborn children, both male and female, were dedicated in the temple. "From her" our Lord Jesus Christ "was born" according to the flesh, through the Holy Spirit, not from the seed of a man nor through bodily union.
The Lord, then, is born of the tribe of Judah, of the seed of David and Abraham according to the flesh, though he is God, in the forty-second year of the reign [?]

Augustus reigned fifty-six years and six months. After him his son Tiberius succeeded to the rule for [?] years. After Tiberius, Gaius reigned three years, nine months and twenty-two days. After Gaius, Claudius reigned [?] years; after Claudius, Nero [?] years; after Nero, Vespasian nine years; after Vespasian, his son Titus two years; after Titus, his brother Domitian [?] years and [?] months; after Domitian, Nerva [?] year and four months; after Nerva, Trajan nineteen years; after Trajan, Hadrian [?]; after Hadrian, Antoninus Pius twenty-two years; after Antoninus, Marcus Aurelius Antoninus, also called Verus, nineteen years. Then came Commodus, [?] years; Pertinax, [?] months; Severus, [?] years; his son Antoninus, seven years; Macrinus, one year; another Antoninus, [?] years; Alexander (not the Macedonian), [?] years; Maximinus, [?] years; Gordian, seven years; Philip, seven years; Decius, [?] year; Gallus [?] and Volusianus, [?] years; [?] years; another Claudius, one year; Aurelian, [?] years; Tacitus, seven months; Probus, [?] years; Carus, Carinus and Numerian, two years; Diocletian, [?] years.

After Diocletian came Maximian, Licinius, Constantius, Constantine, Constans, Constantius and Constantine, Julian, Jovian, Valentinian, Valens and Gratian. From the death of Diocletian to this present year is [?] years. This year is the ninetieth year of Diocletian, the [?] year of Valentinian and Valens, and the [?] year of Gratian. It is the year when Gratian Augustus was consul for the third time with the most illustrious Equitius, in the second indiction.
61. All of us, then, descend in succession from the Adam mentioned above. The order has not been lost, and the things God has done are not to be turned into allegories.

There really is an Adam, then. There really are fig leaves and a fig tree, the tree for knowing what can be known of good and evil, and the tree of life in the middle of paradise. There are a serpent, disobedience and obedience. There are rivers, and there are Eve and the creature that was fashioned.
For "all things are possible with God." He can change corruptible things into incorruption, and he can make things on earth continue in incorruption.
Let no one be amazed at this. He came and showed it himself: he took corruptible flesh, clothed it with the Godhead and displayed it as incorruptible. "For who will bring a charge against" God?

Let us look at another speculation. Scripture says that he drove them out of paradise and set the cherubim and the flaming sword to guard the way to the tree of life. Adam and those with him went out and lived opposite paradise. Let no one be deceived by empty myths.
"For God is able to raise up children from stones." God is also able to change corruptible things into incorruption, and able to create the rest of paradise on earth whenever he wished.
The earth does not belong to one god and heaven to another. All things belong to the same God, and he grants incorruption to each as he wills.

We know that Adam's body too was fashioned from the earth, the same earth our bodies come from, and yet we have the hope of eternal life and of an incorruptible inheritance. The Savior's body too came from Mary, and it has been spiritually united with the incorruption of the Word in heaven.

We have gathered all this and set it down here because we do not wish to cast aside any of the things that are written. We would rather proceed in simplicity and be found faithful toward God in what he has truly written for us. He has given us the way of truth for our salvation. It is fitting to leave to him alone the knowledge of things beyond comprehension.

62. Origen, may God forgive him for filling people with fantasies through his allegories, introduced another fanciful speculation. He claimed that the garments of skin which divine Scripture says God made for Adam and Eve were not garments of skin.

Instead, he says, the "garment of skin" means the fleshly part of the body, or the body itself. After the disobedience, he says, and after they had eaten from the tree, God clothed their souls with these bodies, that is, with this flesh. The whole idea is foolish even to state.
Origen plays the clever sophist and says, "Was God a tanner, then, that he should tan hides and make garments for Adam and Eve?" But such reasoning is far more brutish.

Which was easier for God, to make heaven and earth out of nothing or to make garments of skin? When did he ever will to work his wonders and fail to work them? When has he ever been unable to change lifeless things into living ones?

Moses' rod was dry wood, yet God made it a living serpent that chased Moses, so that Moses fled from it. This showed that what happened was no phantom but real. And how was it that for forty years the people's clothes did not shrivel, their hair did not grow long, and their sandals did not wear out?

Let the fools who followed Origen's derangement on this point tell me this. When the Savior rose from the dead and left the linen cloths in the tomb, as it is written, did he appear naked to the disciples after rising from the dead with body and soul?
When he showed Thomas and those with him his bones and flesh, his hands and his side, he was clearly not naked. So who wove him the clothes he wore after the resurrection?

You will certainly tell me that they were spiritual garments, which he made for himself by his own will. But if he could make such garments for himself, could he not make those garments of skin for Adam and Eve by his own will? Truly

Origen's allegory falls apart. If Adam's flesh was created after he had eaten from the tree, where did God get the rib from before he had eaten? For when Adam woke from his trance he said, "This is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh."
63. "From now on, then, let no one trouble us." This is what the holy church of God has believed from the beginning. Origen will not stand beside us on the day of judgment.

I truly wonder how some people put up with a man who blasphemed his own Master. Let such people read Origen's On First Principles. Let those who think themselves sons of the catholic church learn [?], and let them not dare to separate the [Son?] from the Godhead of the Father.

[?] Origen did not even deign to say that the Son sees the Father! Instead he says, "As the Son cannot see the Father, so the Holy Spirit cannot see the Son," and again, "The angels cannot see the Holy Spirit, and human beings cannot see the angels."
He deceived himself instead, along with those he led astray. But he did not deceive the person who is intelligent and faithful and believes in the truth and in the
spiritual teaching. So stop, Origen, and stop, you disciples of Origen. The apostles and prophets speak the truth, not you and your teacher.

Let the Gnostics stop. They call themselves "knowing," but their ways deserve condemnation. Let the Valentinians, Manichaeans and Marcionites stop, who have gone astray in everything. Let the Arians stop, and the Anomoeans, the Sabellians, the Pneumatics (also called the Pneumatomachians), and the Dimoirites, who mindlessly exclude the mind.

Divine Scripture speaks the truth in everything. But understanding is needed to know that God speaks the truth, to believe him and his words, to recognize what God has graciously given and will give, and to know that the dead will rise in perfection, as he promised. Every heresy lies, because it has not received the Holy Spirit according to the tradition of the fathers in the holy catholic church of God.

64. We will speak about all these things again, as far as our weakness allows. We are the least and humblest of people, yet God has counted us worthy to belong to the holy catholic church of God and to hold to its foundation. So, as far as our limited ability allows, we set out a partial account of everything for those who wish to care for their own life.

What has been said about the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit was quite enough. Still, we want to explain it more fully and clearly, for the delight, safekeeping and full assurance of the faithful. So we will once again gather the testimonies of divine Scripture, to make a rich feast and a joy for the faithful who read this. We will not hesitate to show again how secure and firm our hope in God is. Nothing differs in Father, Son and Holy Spirit. The Holy Trinity is of one rank and of one substance.
We do not take our teaching from some other source or from our own ideas. We take it from our life, that is, from the prophets, from the coming of our Savior and from his love for humankind.

For he came. Our life came, and he showed us the light again when he found us gone astray. We were, indeed we were, sunk in pride and blasphemies, in the likenesses of idols, in the godlessness of evil spirits, steeped in the commands of every evil.

These things were in me against my will. What I wanted I did not do, but what I hated I was driven to do, because sin was working in me in this way. Then the holy Father sent his holy Son, and in his mercy he saved me and rescued me from all my corruptions.

65. "For the grace of our Lord and Savior has appeared, teaching us to renounce ungodliness and worldly desires and to live soberly, justly and godly in this present age, as we await the blessed hope and the appearing of the glory of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ. He gave himself for us to redeem us from all lawlessness and to purify for himself a people of his own, eager to do good works."

"He blotted out the written record that stood against us, with its decrees that opposed us. He took it out of the way, nailing it to the cross. He stripped the principalities and powers, made a public example of them, and triumphed over them in it." "He shattered gates and smashed iron bars," and showed again the light of [?]. He reached out his hand and made a road for us. He showed us the stairway to heaven and counted us worthy to live in paradise again.

So [?] "dwelt among us." He gave us "the righteous requirement of the law" of the Spirit, so that we might know him and know that what concerns him [?] is the beginning and end of life. He has become for us "a law of righteousness," "a law of faith," "a law of the Spirit," free from "the law of the flesh of sin."
Therefore "I delight in the law of God in my inner self." Christ is our inner self, if he truly dwells in us.

By dying he became the way of life for us, "so that those who live might no longer live for themselves, but for him who died for us and was raised," the source of life. "He remembered the oath" sworn many generations before, as David says. "God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself, not counting their trespasses against them."
"For in him all the fullness was pleased to dwell, and through him to reconcile all things to him, making peace through the blood of the cross."
So he came "for the ordering of the fullness of the times," as had been promised to Abraham and the other saints, "to sum up all things in him, things in the heavens and things on earth."

There was division and enmity "in the forbearance of God," but "he reconciled them in the body of his flesh." "He made both one through himself," for "our peace" had come. He broke down "the dividing wall of partition" and abolished in his flesh the enmity, "the law of commandments with its decrees, so that he might create in himself one new man from the two." So the Gentiles became "members of the same body, sharers and fellow heirs of the promise." He commanded, saying, "Come to me, all you who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest."

So, "since I was weak through the flesh," a Savior was sent to me "in the likeness of sinful flesh." He carried out this plan to "redeem" me from slavery, from corruption and from death. And he became for me "righteousness and sanctification and redemption."

He became my righteousness by doing away with sin through faith in him. He became my sanctification by setting me free through water and the Spirit and through his word. He became my redemption by giving himself up for me, his blood the ransom of the true Lamb. He is the atoning sacrifice that cleanses the world and reconciles all things in heaven and on earth, and at the appointed times he fulfills "the mystery hidden from ages and generations."

This same one "will transform the body of our humiliation to be conformed to the body of his glory, by the power that enables him to subject all things to himself," "for in him the whole fullness of the Godhead dwells bodily."

66. Christ, then, is the vessel of wisdom and of the Godhead. As mediator he "reconciles all things to God in himself, not counting sins." By faith in his covenant, promised beforehand by the law and the prophets, he fulfills hidden mysteries. He is proclaimed Son of God and called Son of David, for he is both, God and man, "the mediator between God and men." He is the true "house of God" and "a holy priesthood." He gives the Holy Spirit, who regenerates all things and renews them again for God. For "the Word became flesh and dwelt among us," and "we saw his glory, the glory as of the only-begotten from the Father."

Rain grows together with trees and plants and produces a body, so that each fruit takes on the likeness of its plant. In the olive it becomes rich oil, taking its substance from the tree. In the vine it takes the color of sweet wine. In the fig tree it is sweetened into a fig. In each kind of seed it increases growth according to that kind.

In the same way, I think, the Word of God became flesh in Mary and was found as a man in the seed of Abraham, according to the promise. "For we have found the Messiah, of whom Moses wrote." Moses said, "Let my speech come down like rain," and David, "Let him come down like rain on a fleece, and like drops falling on the [earth]." Wool that takes in the dew increases the growth of the fleece,

and earth that takes in the rain increases the fruit that farmers hope for. At the Master's command it readily offers its own nature to receive the rain, and it is all the more eager to take from him.

In the same way the Virgin Mary, when she said, "How shall I know" "that this will happen to me?", heard, "The Spirit of the Lord will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you. Therefore the holy one born of you will be called the Son of the Most High."

Christ speaks through the angel. The Master refashions himself in his own creature, "taking the form of a servant." Mary draws the Word up into conception, as the earth draws up the rain, and the Word of God shows himself to be holy fruit, taking on the nature of a mortal.

He came from her, who drew him up as the earth and the fleece draw up rain and dew. He is the fruit of true hope, long awaited by the saints. As Elizabeth said, "Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb." The Word took this fruit from humanity, and he suffered although he is beyond suffering.

He is "the living bread that came down from heaven" and gives life. He is the fruit of the true olive tree, the oil of anointing, compounded as Moses prefigured. He is "the true vine," which the Father alone tends, and which has produced for us a cluster of joy.

He is the living water. A thirsty person who takes it will never thirst again; it is "within him, springing up to eternal life." The new farmers took from this water and shared it with the world, but the old farmers dried it up and spoiled it through unbelief.

By his own blood he sanctifies the nations, and by his own Spirit he leads those who are called up to heaven. "So all who are led by his Spirit" live to God. Those who are not are still counted among the dead, and they are called natural, or fleshly, people.

So he commands us to reject the works of the flesh, which are the strongholds of sin, to put to death the members that belong to death through his grace, and to receive the Holy Spirit, whom we did not have. The Spirit gives life to me, who was long dead, and if I do not receive the Spirit I shall die.

For without his Spirit everyone is dead. "If his Spirit is in us, then he who raised him from the dead will give life to our mortal bodies through his Spirit who dwells in us." I think, though, that both dwell in the righteous person, Christ and his Spirit.

67. Christ is believed to be from the Father, God from God. The Spirit is from Christ, or from both, as Christ says: "who proceeds from the Father," and "he will take from what is mine." And Christ is from the Holy Spirit, as the angel's voice says: "for what is in her is from the Spirit." If this is so, then I grasp the mystery that redeems me by faith, by hearing alone, and by love for the one who came to me.

For God knows himself, Christ proclaims himself, and the Holy Spirit reveals himself to the saints. In the holy Scriptures a Trinity is announced to us, and we believe it without prying curiosity and without dispute, from

hearing. From this faith comes the salvation of grace: "righteousness is from faith, apart from works of the law." For it is written that the Spirit of Christ is given through hearing to those who are being saved.

This faith [?] is made known by the voices of the heralds, as I understand it, having been taught from the Scriptures. There are three holy ones, holy together. There are three who exist, existing together. There are three who have form, sharing one form. There are three who act, acting together. There are three who subsist, subsisting together and being with one another. This is called a holy Trinity: three, yet one harmony and one Godhead, of the same substance, the same Godhead and the same subsistence, like from like. The Trinity produces an equal grace of Father and Son and Holy Spirit.

But how this is so is for them alone to teach. "For no one knows the Father except the Son, nor the Son except the Father, and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him." And he reveals him through the Holy Spirit.

So these are three. One is from him, one is from his side, or one is toward him. Each is understood by each person as worthily as they reveal themselves: as light, fire and spirit, and I think in other likenesses seen in visions as well, depending on how worthy the person who receives them is.

God himself in the beginning said, "Let there be light," and there was the visible light. He himself enlightened us to see "the true light, which enlightens everyone coming into the world." David says, "Send out your light and your truth." He is the Lord who said, "In the last days I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh, and their sons and their daughters will prophesy, and their young men will see visions." In this way he shows us three persons of a holy ministry, from a subsistence that is threefold.

68. I say, then, that Christ "became a servant of the circumcision for the sake of God's truth, to fulfil the promises," and that the Holy Spirit serves together with him. For we have learned from the divine Scriptures: Christ is sent from the Father, and the Holy Spirit is sent; Christ speaks in the saints, and the Holy Spirit speaks; Christ heals, and the Holy Spirit heals; Christ sanctifies, and the Holy Spirit sanctifies; Christ baptizes in his name, and the Holy Spirit baptizes.
So the Scriptures say: "You will send forth your Spirit, and you will renew the face of the [?earth]," which is like saying, "You will send out your word and melt them."

"While they were ministering to the Lord and fasting," it says, "the Holy Spirit said, 'Set apart for me Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have called them,'" which is like saying, "But the Lord said, 'Go into the city, and there you will be told what you must do.'"
"So they, sent out by the Holy Spirit, went down to Seleucia," as Christ might say, "Behold, I send you out as sheep in the midst of wolves."
"For it seemed good to the Holy Spirit to lay on you no other burden than these necessary things," as one might say, "I command, not I but the Lord, that a wife should not separate from her husband."

"They went through Phrygia and the region of Galatia, having been forbidden by the Holy Spirit to speak the word in Asia; and when they had come to Mysia, they tried to go into Bithynia, but the Spirit did not allow them," as Christ might say, "Go and baptize all the nations" [?] "Carry no bag, no staff, nor sandals."

"They told Paul through the Spirit," it says, "not to go up to Jerusalem"; or Agabus: "Thus says the Holy Spirit: The man who owns this belt…" This is just as Paul said, "Are you seeking proof of the Christ who speaks in me?" or "Remember the words of the Lord, how he himself said, 'It is good to give rather than to receive.'"
"And now, behold, I am going, [?bound] in the Spirit," as Paul might say, "a prisoner of Jesus Christ."
"Except that the Spirit testifies to me in every city, saying…" is like saying, [?] "The Lord bears witness to my soul that I am not lying."
"In power according to the Spirit of holiness" is like saying, "Holy is he who rests among the holy."
And "circumcision of the heart in the Spirit" is like saying, "And you were circumcised with a circumcision not made with hands, in putting off the body of sins, in the circumcision of Christ."
"If indeed the Spirit of God dwells in you" is like saying, "As you received Christ, walk in him," and "The Spirit of the Lord spoke in me, and his word was in my mouth."
And "having the firstfruits of the Spirit" is like saying, "Christ the firstfruits."
"But the Spirit himself intercedes for us" is like saying, "who is at the right hand of God, who also intercedes for us."
"So that the offering of the Gentiles may be acceptable, sanctified in the Holy Spirit" is like saying, "May the Lord sanctify you, so that you may be pure and blameless for the day of Christ."
"But to us God has revealed it through his Spirit" is like saying, "When he who set me apart from my mother's womb was pleased, through his grace, to reveal his Son in me."
"We have not received the spirit of the world, but the Spirit who is from God" is like saying, "Examine yourselves, whether Christ is in you."
"You are God's temple, and the Spirit of God dwells in you" is like saying, "I will dwell in them and walk among them, and I will be their God, and they shall be my people."

69. But he also speaks of justification and grace as coming from both: "You were justified in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ and in the Spirit of our God," which is like saying, "Having been justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ."

"No one can say 'Jesus is Lord' except in the Holy Spirit," and no one can [?] the Holy Spirit except from the Lord. "There are varieties of gifts, but the same Spirit; and there are varieties of ministries, but the same Lord; and there are varieties of workings, but it is the same God who works all things in all"; and "from glory to glory, as from the Lord, the Spirit."
And "Do not grieve the Holy Spirit, in whom you were sealed for the day of redemption" is like saying, "Or are we provoking the Lord to jealousy? Are we stronger than he?"
