"But the Spirit says expressly" is like saying, "Thus says the Lord Almighty."
And "My Spirit stands in your midst" [?] "If anyone opens to me, I will come in, I and the Father, and we will make our dwelling with him."

And Isaiah says, "and the Spirit of God upon him"; and Christ, "The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me"; and "Jesus of Nazareth, whom God anointed with the Holy Spirit"; or "The Lord has sent me, and his Spirit."
Clear too is the voice of the seraphim, crying, "Holy, holy, holy, Lord of Sabaoth."

And if you hear that "being exalted at the right hand of God and having received from the Father the promise of the Spirit"; or "to wait for the promise of the Father, which you heard"; or that "the Spirit drives him out into the wilderness"; or that he himself says, "Do not worry about what you will say, for it is the Spirit of my Father who speaks in you"; or "But if I cast out demons by the Spirit of God"; or "But whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven," and so on; or "Father, into your hands I will commit my spirit," and so on; or "The child grew and became strong in spirit"; or "Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, returned from the Jordan"; or "Jesus returned in the power of the Spirit"; or "What is born of the Spirit is spirit" (which is like saying, "What came to be in him was life"); or "And I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Advocate, the Spirit of truth"; or "Why has Satan filled your heart" (Peter says to Ananias) "to lie to the Holy Spirit?" and after this, "You have not lied to men but to God." So he is God from God, and the Holy Spirit is God, to whom those who kept back part of the price of the field lied; or "who was manifested in the flesh, justified in the Spirit" — I have nothing greater than this to say.

And the Son [?] is God: "from whom," it says, "is the Christ according to the flesh, who is God over all." "Believe," it says, "in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved"; and "He spoke," it says, "the word of the Lord to them," "and he brought them up into his house and set a table before them, and rejoiced with his whole household, having believed in God"; or that "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God"; or "so that they may adorn the teaching of God our Savior"; or "For the grace of God and Savior has appeared to all people, training us"; or "awaiting the blessed hope and the appearing of the glory of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ."

And the ministry of the Spirit and of the Word is the same: "Take heed," it says, "to yourselves and to all the flock, in which the Holy Spirit has made you overseers, to shepherd the church of God," which is like saying, "I give thanks to Christ Jesus our Lord, who strengthened me, because he judged me faithful, appointing me to ministry."

70. So, as has been shown, the Son and the Holy Spirit work together with the Father: "For by the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the Spirit of his mouth all their host." And the Holy Spirit is to be worshipped: "For those who worship God must worship in spirit and truth."

But if these work together, then a creature does not make a creature, nor does the Godhead become something created, nor is God known within measure or bounds. For he is uncircumscribed, uncontainable, beyond comprehension, encompassing all the works of God.

Nor is the creation to be worshipped: "For they worshipped," it says, "the creature rather than the [?Creator], and became fools." For how is it not folly to call a creature God and to set aside the first commandment, which says, "Hear, O Israel, the Lord your God is one Lord"; "There shall be no new god among you"?

In the holy Scriptures various names are given to the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit: to the Father, Father Almighty, Father of all, Father of Christ; to the Son, Word, Christ, true Light; and to the Holy Spirit, Advocate, Spirit of truth, Spirit of God, Spirit of Christ.

Further, then, God the Father is understood as light — but as surpassingly bright light — as power, wisdom, [life]. And if God the Father is light, the Son is light from light, and he it is who "dwells in unapproachable light."

God is wholly power, and therefore [the Son] is "Lord of powers"; God is wholly wisdom, and so the Son is wisdom from wisdom, "in whom all the treasures of wisdom are hidden"; God is wholly life, and so the Son is life from life: "For I am the truth and the life."
And the Holy Spirit is from both, Spirit from Spirit. For "God is spirit"; [?] of the Godhead, he is the giver of gifts, most true, enlightening, the Advocate, the herald of the Father's counsels.

For as the Son is "the Angel of great counsel," so also is the Holy Spirit. "But we have received," it says, "the Spirit of God, so that we may know the things freely given us by God, which we also speak, not in persuasive words of wisdom, but in demonstration of the Spirit of God, comparing spiritual things with spiritual."

71. But someone will say: "Then do we say there are two sons? And how is he only-begotten?" Nay rather, "who are you to answer back to God?" For he calls the one who is from himself the Son, and the one who is from both the Holy Spirit — and these, understood by the saints through faith alone, are luminous and light-giving, have a luminous operation, and are in harmony with the "Father of lights" himself. Hear in faith, my friend,

that the Father is Father of a true Son, wholly light, and the Son is [Son] of a true Father, light, not in name only as things made or created are; and the Holy Spirit is the Spirit of truth, a third light from the Father and the Son.

All other things are so by adoption or by calling, not like these in operation or power or light or understanding; as when one says, "I have begotten sons and raised them up," or as when one says, "I said, You are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High," or as when one says, "who has begotten the drops of dew," or as when one says, "from whom every family in heaven and on earth [is named]," or as when one says, "I am he who establishes the thunder and creates spirit."

For the true Father is not like other fathers or patriarchs, beginning to be a father or at some point in time ceasing to be a father. For if he begins to be a father, then he was once the son of another father before he became Father of the Only-begotten; and on the same pattern fathers are thought of as children of fathers, and one would have to search to infinity to find the true father at the head of the lineage.
Nor is the true Son, like other children by adoption, new to being a son. For if he were new to being a son, there was once a time when the Father was not Father of the Only-begotten.
Nor is the Spirit of truth, like other spirits, created or made; nor is "the Angel of great counsel" so called in the way the other angels are.

For some have a beginning and an end, while others have a beginning and a dominion beyond conception; some create all things for endless ages, working together with the Father, while others are created by them as they will; some worship these, while the others are worshipped by all creatures; some heal the things that are made, while others receive healing from them; some are judged according to their deserts, while others hold just judgment;

some are in time, while others are not in time; some enlighten all things, while others are enlightened by them; some call infants to the heights, while others are called by the Perfect One; some bestow grace on all, while others receive gifts; and, in a word, the one sings the praise of holiness in the heavens of heavens and the other invisible places, while the others, being praised, worthily grant their gifts to the worthy.
72. Scripture speaks of very many spirits: "He who makes his angels spirits and his ministers a flame of fire," and "Let all spirits praise the Lord."

To the worthy is given the gift of "discernment of spirits." For some are heavenly, "rejoicing in the truth"; some are earthly, given to deceit and error; and some are under the earth, children of the abyss and of darkness. For the Gospel says, "they begged him not to send them away into the abyss." Likewise he rebuked the spirits, drove out spirits with a word, and "would not allow them to speak."

There is said to be "a spirit of judgment and a spirit of burning"; there is also said to be a spirit of the world ("We have not received the spirit of the world," it says), and the spirit of a man: "For who among men knows the things of a man except the spirit of the man?" and "a spirit that goes and does not return"; "for a spirit passed through it, and it shall be no more"; and "You will take away their spirit, and they will fail"; and there is a spirit of the prophets:

"The spirits of the prophets," it says, "are subject to the prophets"; and "Behold, a lying spirit stood before the Lord, and he said to it, 'By what means will you deceive Ahab?' And, 'I will be,' it says, 'a lying spirit in the mouth of the prophets.'"

There is said to be also "a spirit of stupor" and "a spirit of cowardice" and "a spirit of Python," "a spirit of fornication" and "a spirit of the tempest" and "a spirit of many words" and "a spirit of infirmity" and "an unclean spirit" and "a deaf spirit" and "a mute spirit" and "a stammering spirit" and "an exceedingly fierce spirit," which is called Legion, and "the spiritual forces of wickedness."

To the wise the sayings about spirits are countless. But just as the many are sons by adoption or by calling and not in truth, because they have a beginning and an end [?] and are liable to sin, so too very many are spirits by adoption or by calling, even if they are sinful; but the Holy Spirit alone is called the Spirit of the Father and of the Son, "the Spirit of truth" and "the Spirit of God" and "the Spirit of Christ" and "the Spirit of grace."

For he bestows what is good on each in different ways: "to one a spirit of wisdom, to another a spirit of knowledge, to another a spirit of strength, to another a spirit of healings, to another a spirit of prophecy, to another a spirit of discernment, to another tongues, to another interpretations," and the rest of the gifts, as it says, "one and the same Spirit, distributing to each as he wills."

"Your good Spirit will lead me, O God," says David; or "The Spirit blows where he wills" (showing us by such words that the Holy Spirit has real subsistence), "and you hear his voice, but you do not know where he comes from or where he goes"; and "unless you are born of water and the Spirit," just as Paul said, "For in Christ Jesus I begot you."

Of him the Lord says: "When the Advocate comes, whom I will send to you, the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father, he will bear witness about me"; and "I still have many things to say, but you cannot bear them now. When he, the Spirit of truth, comes, he will guide you into all the truth. For he will not speak on his own, but whatever he hears he will speak, and he will declare to you the things that are to come. He will glorify me, for he will take from what is mine and declare all things to you."

73. If, then, he proceeds from the Father and, as the Lord says, "will take from what is mine," then just as "no one has known the [Father] except the [Son], nor the Son except the Father," so I dare to say that no one knows the Spirit except the Son, from whom he receives, and the Father, from whom he proceeds; and no one knows the Son and the Father

except the Holy Spirit, who truly glorifies, who teaches all things, who bears witness about the Son, who is from the Father, who is of the Son, the only guide to truth, interpreter of the holy laws, instructor in the spiritual law, master of the prophets, teacher of the apostles, the light of the Gospel's doctrines, the one who chooses the saints, true light from true light.
The Son is a natural son, a true son, a genuine son, the only one from the only one; and with him is also the Spirit, [not called son] but named Spirit.

This is God, glorified in the Church: Father always, Son always, and Holy Spirit always, most high [from] most high, and spiritual [?] spiritual, having a glory beneath which are created and made things — in short, the whole universe, each thing measured and contained.

One Godhead is proclaimed above all in Moses, a duality is preached emphatically in the prophets, and the Trinity is made manifest in the Gospels, fitting itself more fully, through the times and generations, to the righteous for knowledge and faith. Knowledge of it is immortality, and from faith in it comes adoption as sons.

First it sets forth ordinances of the flesh in Moses, as though raising up the outer enclosure of the temple; second, it explains ordinances of the soul in the rest of the prophecies, as though adorning the holy place; third, ordinances of the spirit in the Gospels, as though setting in order the mercy seat and the holy of holies for its own dwelling: a holy tabernacle, a holy temple, [which]

[?] the righteous man alone, who is joined with these [?]. And in him dwells one Godhead infinite, one Godhead incorruptible, one Godhead inconceivable, incomprehensible, ineffable, invisible, alone knowing itself, manifesting itself to whom it wills, raising up witnesses to itself, calling, predestining, glorifying, lifting up out of Hades, sanctifying, uniting again to its own glory and faith these threes: things heavenly, earthly and under the earth; spirit, soul, flesh; faith, hope, love; past, present, future; age of age, ages of ages, sabbaths of sabbaths; circumcision of the flesh, circumcision of the heart, "the circumcision of Christ in putting off the body of sins." And altogether it purifies for itself

all things, invisible and visible, thrones, dominions, principalities, authorities, powers; and in all is the same holy voice, crying from glory to glory, "Holy, holy, holy," [glorifying] the Father in the Son and the Son in the Father, with the Holy [Spirit], to whom be glory and power for ever and ever. Amen. And whoever believes thus will say: So be it, so be it.

74. Concerning the Trinity and the consubstantiality of God the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, we who are weak and unlearned, devising nothing clever and not entrusting ourselves to "the trickery of men," but rather gathering testimonies from the divine Scriptures, have collected them in part for those who wish it, so that the faithful may find them and the misbelieving and vainglorious may be refuted. For great is the power of faith in the Holy Spirit,

proclaimed in various ways throughout all the divine Scriptures [?]. But since the security of our salvation is the sure [?faith] and confirmation of hope concerning the incarnation of our Savior and his coming in the flesh, and concerning the resurrection of the dead and our regeneration, we ourselves once again add a little to this labor of ours, for those who wish to study more closely, and we continue, gathering from the same divine Scriptures and adding to our discourse.

For since, as we have already been taught in what was written above, our Lord himself in his Gospel said to his disciples, "Go and baptize all the nations in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to keep the commandments that I have commanded you" [?] — he himself, the holy Word, truly subsisting, who came forth from the Father, through whom the ages came into being, through whom times and seasons came to be.

For there was neither season nor time before the Son. For if there was time before the Son, then time is greater than the Son; and how then is it true that "all things came into being through him, and without him nothing came into being that has come into being"? For if anything has come into being, it came into being through him, while he himself is uncreated and ever-existing; for the Father always was, and his Holy Spirit always was.

For if there was time before the Son, then [another] must again be sought through whom the time before the Son came to be, and from there our reasoning will be turned to countless things, to fantasies lurking within human opinion, or rather to a fornication of thoughts, and not [?] to soundness of mind.

There was, then, no time before the Son, since the Son did not come into being through times; rather, through the Son came times and the angels and all other creatures. There was never a time when the Son was not, nor was there ever a time when the Spirit was not.

75. Some people misread the passage and, not understanding it, think they should punctuate it at the words "All things came into being through him, and without him nothing came into being," putting the stop there. From this they take up a blasphemous suspicion against the Holy Spirit. They are wrong about the reading, and from that error in reading they stumble and turn to blasphemy.

The reading goes like this: "All things came into being through him, and without him nothing came into being that has come into being in him." That is, if anything has come into being, it came into being through him.

So the Father always was, and the Son always was, and the Spirit breathes forth from the Father and the Son. Neither is the Son created nor is the Spirit created. But everything after the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit is created and originated. These things did not exist, and they came into being from the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, through the ever-existing Word together with the ever-existing Spirit.
Through this Word, then, all created things came into being: through the heavenly King, the subsistent Word, our Savior and benefactor.

For the Savior himself came down from the holy [?] heavens of heavens. In the virgin's workshop he saw fit to accomplish our salvation. He was born a second time, of Mary, conceived through the Holy Spirit. He took flesh; he is the Word who became flesh without changing his nature. Together with his Godhead he took manhood. Being perfect from the Father, he fulfilled the perfect dispensation. He came into the world for us and for our [?]. He took flesh and a human soul,
and, being perfect from the Father, he became man among us, not in appearance but in truth. Through the Holy Spirit he refashioned a perfect man into himself from Mary, the Mother of God.

He did not dwell in a man, as he used to speak in the prophets and dwell and work in them with power. Instead the Word himself became flesh. He was not changed from being God, nor did he convert the Godhead into manhood. Rather, together with the very fullness of his own Godhead and the very hypostasis of God the Word, who is subsistent, he took into himself being man and whatever man is.

This means a perfect man, [having] all that is in a man and being such as a man is. The Only-begotten came and took this man so that, being God, he might perfectly accomplish the whole of salvation in the perfect man. He left nothing of the man out, so that the part left out would not become [?] food for the devil.

76. Some weave in fables and turn Scripture into myths, saying that he took flesh only and not a soul, on the basis of the saying "But we have the mind of Christ." Let them learn from that very saying that those who said "But we have the mind of Christ" had their own minds and had not spat them out. They had their own minds together with the mind of Christ, and both were at work: the mind of Christ was able to improve them, and their own minds understood rightly.
Let them recognize that the same is true of Christ. He was God and was mind in himself, yet he had the mind of a man [?] and took a soul along with the flesh.

So the mind did not lead him astray as it does a mere man. Instead he himself became the mind's orderer, corrector and improver. For just as he took the flesh without being overcome by the flesh, so too he took the mind without being overcome by the mind.

On the contrary, then, such people fall badly into an even greater contradiction. For throughout the divine Scriptures plainly cry out hard sentences, and they pronounce them not against the mind but against the flesh.

"For the fruits of the flesh," it says, "are fornication, adultery, licentiousness and the like." And: "Those who are in the flesh cannot please God." And: "The flesh desires against the Spirit." But about the mind it says, "I will sing with the spirit, and I will sing with the mind too," and "My mind is unfruitful or fruitful." For God appointed the mind, which Scripture usually calls the heart, as governor, so to speak, and charioteer of the whole vessel. It discerns between good and evil and tests whatever arises within us. "For the mind discerns words, as the throat tastes food." The mind in a man is able to discern, but it does not yet consent unless it gives itself over to change.

77. Why, then, did some decide to exclude the mind from the Lord's incarnation? What good did they do to life by turning it toward [?] disorder instead? Or how did the mind harm or benefit us, so to speak, that they should come to Christ's aid? Or was it to do him this great favor, saying of him that he did not take a mind?

"Galatians" are "mindless," and "Cretans are always liars," and "Ephraim is a mindless dove." But when our Lord became man and entered life, he took up everything perfectly. Or rather, he took it himself, having become the fashioner of his own body. He himself took the soul for himself, or rather placed it in himself.
Some people want to make Christ's coming in the flesh deficient, and the perfect dispensation in him as well. With I know not what in mind, they have wrongly said that Christ did not take a mind.

Yet they plainly do not [?] the mind [?]. For they think the mind is a hypostasis, and they dare to say that by nature it is what Scripture usually calls the spirit in man. As the apostle says, "that your spirit and soul and body may be kept whole in the day of our Lord Jesus Christ."

So they are wrong. Suppose the spirit is mind and the mind is spirit, as they themselves think, and the soul is another [hypostasis] besides the mind and the spirit. Then there are no longer two things in man brought together into one hypostasis, the soul alone being subsistent and the body subsistent. Instead we now find four: the mind one hypostasis, the soul another, the spirit another and the body another.

And if we look further, there will be even more. For man has many names, such as "the inner man" and "the outer man." Scripture has used all these terms as concepts, holding our understanding tightly together, so that we leave out nothing that belongs to salvation and have no excuse to stray from the matter at hand. All these things are in man, but there is no need to pry into them too curiously.

Still, let us follow their reasoning. If the mind is the spirit and the spirit is the mind, and these exist [?] apart from the soul, then what does he mean when he says, "I will sing with the spirit, I will sing with the mind too"? By saying this he showed that the spirit is not the mind and the mind is not the spirit.

78. Again, "The soul that sins shall die" does not speak of a soul apart from the body. [Or again,] "For there were," it says, "seventy souls," and these were certainly not souls without bodies but bodies with souls. Common usage also tends to speak of people by a single term, saying that a man is master of eighty bodies, and these are certainly not without souls.

So the Word who became flesh [was] not without a soul, [just as] he was not without the whole reality [of manhood]. When Scripture says "soul," it does not mean a soul without a body, and when we speak of him we do not think of him as being without a soul.

What, then, possessed those who want to say that the mind was excluded? How did this benefit the church? Or rather, how did it fail to throw it into confusion? And how can anyone who thinks such things avoid making our salvation deficient?

For we cannot think of the mind as anything separate, nor can we call it a hypostasis on its own. It is rather the composite, rational and thinking faculty in each person who has [not] gone astray. To give an illustration [?]: as the eyes are in the body, so the mind is in the soul. Again, we do not say even this to be contentious, but simply [to describe] the faculty of understanding in human beings [?].
What, then, is man? Soul, body, mind, and whatever else there is. What did the Lord come to save? Certainly the perfect man. Therefore he took everything in man perfectly.
Otherwise, how were these things fulfilled in him? They were prophesied and attributed to him as man, with respect to mind, body, soul and the whole incarnation, yet without sin.

For the divine word clearly teaches us this when it says, "Behold, my servant shall understand, my beloved, whom I have chosen, in whom my soul is well pleased; I will put my Spirit [upon him]," and what follows. To what, then, does "understanding" apply? If to the Godhead, does the Godhead then lack understanding? Far from it! This is fulfilled in the Lord's humanity. But if it has been fulfilled in the Lord's humanity, how could an incarnation without a mind understand? That is impossible.

If "shall understand" refers to Christ at all, then it refers to the Word from above, who became flesh from Mary, became man and "lived among" us, as it is written. So he undoubtedly took on the dispensation together with the mind, since understanding belongs to it.

This is why the Gospel says of him, "He advanced in wisdom and stature." It was not the Godhead that gained stature or lacked wisdom, since the Godhead is Wisdom itself. Rather, it was the Savior's manhood that advanced in wisdom. It was not without a mind, since [otherwise] it could not have done so. And it advanced in stature as the child grew, and this is literally true.

79. But suppose that, because he took a mind, this [?] is thought to mean sin. Then all the more, if we grant that he took flesh, without which sin is not committed ("for the works of the flesh are evident"), we would certainly have to grant that he also sinned in the flesh, since he took the flesh. "For I know," says the apostle, "that nothing good dwells in me, that is, in my flesh."

But who will dare to say that, because the Savior took flesh, he was dragged along with the flesh? He did not carry out the works of the flesh, [but] carried out what fitted the proper order of his whole vessel. He likewise had a [good] flesh. It was human flesh, yet it stumbled in nothing.

For God the Word came forth from the Father above and was pleased to be in flesh, and he kept the vessel bridled. If he wanted to restrain it from every useless fleshly act, he could; and if he wanted, he gave way. He gave way to the bodily needs that were reasonable and fitting for his Godhead.

He had the mind in truth, just as he had the whole incarnation in truth, yet his mind did not reach out toward irrational desires. Nor did he do or think the things of the flesh as we do. Instead, as God who had come in true flesh from the Virgin Mary, he acted [?] with flesh, soul, mind and the whole vessel. He was God the Word, subsistent, from the Father above, who had come to dwell among the human race.

But let no one quibble that this is said loosely, like "Understand my cry." That phrase is used loosely, as a prayer. But it is clear that this usage was prophesied as a sign of his coming in the flesh, and "he advanced in stature" is literally true.

80. But what do such people think we are saying? If we say that Christ became a perfect man from Mary, or that he had [a mind], are we to suspect that he fell into sins? Far from it! "For he committed no sin, and no deceit was found in his mouth."

He breathed his power into the saints, and those into whom he breathed it are attested to have been holy, righteous, advanced in their days and blameless. How much more, then, the Word himself, "in whom all the fullness of the Godhead was pleased to dwell bodily"! He took true flesh from Mary the ever-virgin, a truly human soul, a mind and whatever else there is in man. Yet, having them all in himself, as God he held them firm. They were not divided toward evil, not broken down by the evil one, not captured by pleasure, not subject to Adam's transgression.

This is why the apostle says, "born of a woman, born under the law," and again, "being found in form as a man." Taken together, "in form," "as a man," "born" and "under the law" signify perfection and freedom from passion. From "born" we learn that he is perfect; from "under the law," that he was not merely an appearance; from "in form," that his shape was real; and from "as a man," that he was sinless.

Since these things are so, let no one be deceived by empty myths. If he was truly begotten from the Father above, he was [truly] born from Mary as well. He is true above and true below. If he is imperfect below, he is imperfect above too. But if he is perfect above, he is perfect below too. He did not dwell in some other perfect [man], but perfected all things in himself.

And he rose from the dead. He was no longer divided, with his body in the tomb and his Godhead and soul in the underworld. He was no longer subject to touch, no longer held back. He entered when the doors were shut, yet Thomas handled him, so that he would not be taken for an apparition but [known] in truth.

Thomas believed in him once what had been foretold was fulfilled: "With my hands I sought God, and I was not deceived." He is the same God and the same man. He did not cause any confusion, but blended the two into one.

He did not pass into nonexistence. Instead he empowered the earthly body together with the Godhead, united it into one power and gathered it into one Godhead. He is one Lord, one Christ, not two Christs or two Gods [?].

In him is a spiritual body, and in him an incomprehensible Godhead. What suffered was not corrupted; what is impassible is incorruptible; the whole is incorruption. He is God and Lord, seated at the right hand of the Father. He did not leave the flesh behind, but united it into one, and the whole is seated as one Godhead at the right hand of the Father.

81. This, then, is the Only-begotten: perfect, uncreated, unchangeable, unalterable, inconceivable and invisible. He became man, rose spiritually and "dies no more." He is no longer poor, he who "though he was rich became poor for our sake." He is wholly spirit and unites the fleshly and the divine. He is one Lord, King and Christ, the Son of God, seated in heaven at the Father's right hand, "above every rule and authority and power, and every name that is named." He says in the Gospel, "Go and baptize all the nations in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit."

And this, set in the middle [?], did not signify that the Son was fused with the Father, [or that the Holy Spirit was fused with the Father and the Son]. Rather, he knows a true Father, and he showed that he himself is a true and subsistent Word, and that his Holy Spirit is a subsistent Spirit and "the Spirit of truth," uncreated, unchangeable and unalterable. He did not say it
so that anyone could form a false notion [?], approaching the faith deceitfully, hiding his feet and playing false with the truth ("for God searches hearts and reins").

Yet the heretic says, "Of course I believe that the Father is Father, the Son is Son and the Holy Spirit is Holy Spirit, and I confess three hypostases in one essence. I do not call the essence something different from the Godhead, nor the Godhead something different from the essence. We speak of [one] essence for the sake of precision, so that we do not speak of a different form of the Godhead of the Trinity."

For, as I said, such a man hides himself and speaks craftily and deceitfully again: "I believe that the Father is Father, the Son is Son, the Holy Spirit is Holy Spirit." But he holds a hidden notion like this. He pictures the divine on the model of ourselves and says to himself, "As I have a human body, soul and spirit, so does the Godhead:
the Father is, so to speak, the form; the Son is like the soul in a man; and the Spirit is like the breath that blows through a man."

For some people act deceitfully and think of the Godhead in this way. But that is not what we have been taught. Look: the Father bears witness from heaven with a voice; the Son is in the Jordan; and the Spirit takes shape and descends in the form of a dove. The Spirit took shape on its own, being a hypostasis in its own right. It is not different from the Father's and the Son's but of the same essence, a hypostasis from a hypostasis; Father, Son and Holy Spirit are of the same essence.

[And] again, look: the Father sits in heaven [?]. But do not take "sits" in a human sense; hold it as something indescribable and incomprehensible. And Scripture did not say "The Son went up to the Father," but "He sat down at the right hand of the Father."

Again, the Only-begotten taught about the Holy Spirit, saying, "I am going away, and he will come, the Holy Spirit, the Spirit of truth. If I do not go away, he does not come." If the Spirit were fused with the Son himself, he would not have said "I am going away and he is coming." He said it to show one hypostasis and another hypostasis. Yet there is one Godhead, one God, one truth.

82. So I have written this for whoever wishes [?] to know the order of our life and our sure confession. It has been kept unstained in the catholic church from the Law, the Prophets, the Gospels and the Apostles, and from the times of the apostles until our own times.

From time to time, out of envy and to unsettle the one true faith, the heresies have persecuted this faith, hope and salvation of ours. Yet it has held fast in its truth, while in every age the heresies defile themselves and cut themselves off from the church.

Recently, for instance, we hear again of certain men who are thought to hold first rank among some of the ascetics in Egypt, the Thebaid and other regions. They think like the Hieracites and say that there is a resurrection of our flesh, but not of this flesh; rather, of some other flesh in its place. Such people have gone astray and turned God's truth and our sure hope into myths. That is why we are forced to speak about this subject once more.
83. Unbelievers deny resurrection altogether. Misbelievers, by thinking about the resurrection in this way, have fallen away from the true hope in a careless and senseless fashion.

The Greeks are the ones who deny the resurrection completely, because of the impiety of the many lawless deeds committed among them. They hate the resurrection because of the shame they will suffer at it, since they have not known God or his commandments. Yet they will rise, whether they want to or not.

For creation itself plainly refutes them, showing a figure of the resurrection every day. The day sets, and we glimpse the condition of the dead, as night hints at sleep. The day rises, waking us and showing the sign of resurrection.

Fruits are picked and standing crops are cut down, a picture of our departure from this world. The earth is sown and sprouts, [showing] that what is buried after the reaping will rise again. The locust dies after burying in the earth the offspring it has laid, and after a time the earth gives back what was buried. The seeds of the crops are sown; first they die, then they come to fruition.

"For unless it dies, it is not made alive." God has placed seals of resurrection in us in our ten and ten nails, testifying to our hope. And he has proclaimed our resurrection through the hair, as with a crown on the head. For the parts of us that seem to be dead body, that is, hair and nails, grow again after they are cut each day, signifying the hope of the resurrection.

84. Countless examples could be given to convince unbelievers. But neither the ring-dove among birds nor the dormouse among animals has persuaded them. The dormouse is dead for six months and the ring-dove for forty days, and after these periods they come back to life.

When beetles are about to die, they hide themselves in a ball of dung, bury the ball in the earth and cover it over. Then they are found again, coming back to life from their own moisture and from their very remains.

There is no need for me to speak about the phoenix, the Arabian bird, since many believers and unbelievers have already heard of it. Its story seems to be this. When it reaches its five-hundredth year and knows that the time of its death has come, it builds a nest of spices. It carries this to the Egyptian city called Heliopolis, which in the Egyptian and Hebrew languages is called On. There it beats its breast many times with its own wings,
brings fire out of its body and sets alight the material laid in the place. In this way it burns itself as a whole burnt offering and is reduced to ashes, all its [?] together with its bones.
But by God's dispensation a cloud is sent. It rains and puts out the flame that has consumed the bird's body, though by then the bird is already dead and thoroughly roasted.

Once the flame is out, remnants of its flesh are left, still raw. Within one day they decay and produce a worm. The worm grows wings and becomes a chick, and on the third day it is full-grown. Once grown, it shows itself to the attendants of the place, then hurries back to its homeland and rests.

85. I am moved to marvel at the minds of the unbelieving Greeks and other barbarians, deceived as they are in everything. In their own myths they are not ashamed to point to resurrection in every way, and they often sing about resurrection.

Their myths record that Alcestis, the daughter of Pelias, died for her husband Admetus and was raised by Heracles after three days and brought back up from the depths. They also record that Pelops, the son of Tantalus, [was brought back] after his own father cut him up and served him as meat to their falsely named gods.

Amphiaraus son of Oecles was brought back to life by Asclepius. Glaucus son of Minos was revived with a certain herb by Polyidus son of Coeranus. Castor came back through his brother Polydeuces, who willingly chose to exchange life with him on alternate days. And Protesilaus came back through Laodamia.

They also say that Sisyphus and Tantalus, the daughters of Caucasus whom they call the Erinyes, and Tiresias with them have been cast down into Tartarus to pay the penalty there, one by means of a rock, another under a wheel. Others are punished in other ways and are still under punishment, since they have not passed into nonexistence but exist in bodies.
If they had no bodies, how could they be handed over to punishment under a rock and a wheel? There is much more that could be said about these things to establish our faith and to refute them.

86. Those who set out from the heresies also sing a song akin to theirs, in harmony with their unbelief. Some of the heretics (the Manichaeans, I mean) say that there will be a resurrection not of the body but of the soul. The Greeks mentioned above think and hold the same view, so their argument is idle chatter rather than something put forward with understanding.

For if the heresies speak of a resurrection and believe in a resurrection at all, but define it as a resurrection of souls, such a view is foolish. How will a soul rise when it has not fallen? We do not bury souls in tombs, but bodies.
For it is not souls that fall but flesh, which is why common usage calls dead bodies "the fallen." So if they acknowledge a resurrection, it is plain to anyone that

it is a resurrection not of the soul but of the body that has fallen. The Greeks who deny the resurrection are refuted in their turn. On the days they call public festivals they carry food and drink to the tombs, burn the food as offerings and pour out the wine as libations. They do the dead no good at all and rather harm themselves.
Yet their custom forces them to confess the resurrection of the dead. They come to the place where the bodies of the departed were laid and call out to the buried dead by name:

"Arise, so-and-so," they say, "eat and drink and be merry." If they think that the souls stay on in the place where the remains of the departed are buried, then this expectation about them is a good one. For the souls are waiting for the coming day and the resurrection of the new birth, until they receive back their bodies, to which they are joined and yoked. And this holds even though the children of the Greeks loathe the flesh as worthless, as utterly perishing and as having no hope of coming back to life.

But if that is not what they mean by doing this, then on what reasoning do they bind souls, which are better than the substance of bodies, to tombs? By their supposition they rather condemn them, ruling that they must keep watch beside the remains of the dead. Or let them tell us: in expectation of what hope do they come?

They may say that they do not think the souls are in the tombs, but in certain storehouses that God has assigned to each soul according to the worth of what it did and how it lived in this life, while the bodies are those that each person has laid with his own hands, the bodies of his neighbours, in the receptacles for bodies, or rather for bones. But it would be foolish for everyone to share this one supposition and what follows from it, since it is acknowledged on every side, and yet for the unbelievers to deny the truth and fail to hold firmly as their hope the things that are possible with God.
87. But I think enough has been said about these matters, since we have set out a few examples out of many.

Then there are those who seem to be Christians but follow Origen. They confess the resurrection of the dead, both of our flesh and of that holy body of the Lord which was taken from Mary, but they say that this flesh is not raised and that God gives another in its place. How could we not say that their view is more impious than the others, and more foolish than the notion held among the Greeks and the remaining heresies?

First of all, if another flesh is raised instead of this one, as they argue, then by their myth God's judgment is not just. It would be judging other flesh in place of the flesh that sinned, or bringing another body to the glory of inheriting the kingdom of heaven in place of the body that toiled in fasts and vigils and persecutions for the name of God.

And how, as the heresies argue, will the soul be judged alone, without the body that sinned with it being present? Such a soul would answer back to God's judgment, claiming that the sins were the body's.

By the reasoning of those who are driven by contentiousness and not by truth, it even has a proof. For it can say: "It was not I who sinned, but the body. Since I left the body I have not fornicated or committed adultery. I have not stolen, I have not murdered, I have not worshipped idols, and I have done nothing evil or beyond remedy."
And its defence will be found reasonable. If it defends itself reasonably, what shall we say? Is God's judgment idle, then? Is God "unjust to inflict wrath" on human beings? "By no means!"

88. But we know that "all things are possible for God." He can bring a body without a soul. If he wishes, he can make bodies that have vanished come back to life and move of themselves without [a soul], as he already did when he carried out such a dispensation through the most holy Ezekiel.

For he said to the holy prophet: "Say, son of man, that bone be gathered to bone and joint to joint." And God's power was a thing to marvel at. The souls had not yet been put in and the bones were still dry. Yet at God's command they not only had the power to move, but were also filled with understanding and with no ordinary knowledge.

For the bones that belong with the feet [?] did not absent-mindedly walk off to the parts near the head, and the vertebrae of the neck did not stray around the ankle joints looking for their place. Each of the bones moved and went with understanding and joined itself to its own joint.
So if God wills, he can raise even a body without a soul. In this he showed his power: by his command to Ezekiel he first brought back to life what people had despaired of.

And he did not say, "Say, son of man, that the spirit is to come first." First, for the sake of faith, he made the difficult part easy, I mean the gathering of the bodies, and only then did he command the souls to enter those very bodies. "And there rose up," it says, "a great assembly."
I have said, then, that God is able to bring even a body back to life without a soul, as was shown above. But the body cannot be judged by itself, for it has a just defence against God's judgment.

It too will speak up and say: "The sin came from the soul. I was not the cause. Since I was dissolved and the soul left me, have I committed adultery, have I fornicated, have I stolen, have I worshipped idols, have I committed any such offence?" And by the reasoning of the contentious, God's judgment will come to nothing.

Therefore, since body and soul were one composite human being made by God, the just Judge raises the body again and gives its soul back into it. In this way God's judgment will be just, because both will share, either in the punishment for sin or in the reward that is to be paid to the saints for virtue and godliness.

89. We believe that this is enough to establish the truth of our hope, and we have set out a few proofs in place of many. But because of those who say that a different body rises in place of the one that falls, we take up the labour again. We wish to benefit those who are willing to understand and are not trying to lose their own life.

May it be that we, the least and the worthless, should labour, so that we ourselves and everyone else may benefit and may not deny the resurrection of our flesh. For in it lies the whole treasure, the foundation of all sober thinking, and the hope of every good work, as it is said: "We have this treasure in earthen vessels," and so on.
For we who are weak practise self-control, and we who are lowly keep ourselves pure. We who have no means long to give alms, so that we may receive what we hope for, the resurrection of the dead.

This is how the rule is founded: the rule of faith and of hope in God, of love, and of martyrdom for the name of God amid persecutions, tortures and other inhuman punishments. It is founded in those who do not deny the resurrection of our flesh, but believe that the very thing that is sown in the

earth will be raised. The divine Scriptures have given us two clear and true testimonies. Through them we can know the hope of our resurrection and not be led astray by the myths of vainglorious men, who were deceived themselves and have written deceit into the world. I will not use many testimonies (and there are not a few in the New and Old Testaments about our hope and resurrection). Instead I will say this briefly:

90. if what is raised were something else, as some claim, the apostle would not have firmly declared, "For this perishable body must put on imperishability, and this mortal body must put on immortality."

We must also be established in our hope concerning the saints, and how they will be made radiant and transformed after the resurrection (as it says, "it is raised in glory"). For that reason holy Scripture says: "Fool! What you sow does not come to life unless it dies. And what you sow is not the body that is to be, but [?] a grain, perhaps of wheat or of some other seed, and God gives it a body as he has chosen." He said this with reference to the glory of those who are raised in radiance.

And to show that it is the very same grain that takes on the glory, the one who also "spoke in Paul" about the resurrection said in his own person in the Gospel: "Unless the grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies," he says, "it remains alone;

but if it dies, it bears many grains." So the apostle spoke of a grain, and the Saviour displayed the same grain of the body in himself. What then shall we say? Did not the very thing that was sown, his own body, the grain, rise? Or was what rose from the tomb after three days something other, something that came from it?

As the angels say: "He has risen; he is not here." As he says to Mary: "Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to my Father." And as he shows his hands and his side to Thomas, saying: "Do not be unbelieving, but believing."

It belongs to unbelievers to say that he did not rise at all, and to those with false belief to say that it was not the very thing that existed and fell asleep that rose. But it belongs to believers to say that the very body rose, and that from that same body which he raised, ours has been established in the hope of truth.

91. This is why he also left the marks of the nails and did not wipe them away, nor [?] the mark of the spear, even though he came in when the doors were shut. For his fleshly body rose spiritual. It was not something other than what it was, but that very thing, united with the Godhead and adorned with the fineness of spirit.

For if it had not had the fineness of spirit, what opening could have let in a bulky body? He came in when the doors were shut to show that this very perishable body of ours truly puts on imperishability (and though it is mortal, it puts on immortality). He was showing the coarse made fine, the mortal made immortal, and the perishable made imperishable.

But he also wanted to refute all who disbelieve in our resurrection, I mean the resurrection. So although he changed the body into fineness and blended the flesh with spirit, after the resurrection he did not wipe away the scars of the nails or the mark of the spear.

Instead he showed that it was the very body that had suffered on the cross. What rose was not something else, nor something else that had sprung from it. It was the very thing that suffered, now beyond suffering, and the very grain that fell, now risen, and risen imperishable.

And again, lest we think that only some part of it was raised, [?] the whole of it did not see corruption, for it says, "You will not let your holy one see corruption," and the whole of it rose, for it says, "He has risen; he is not here."

If he was raised and is not here, he truly rose, and the Scriptures, which are our life, do not err. And so that the deceived might find no pretext, he showed bones and flesh to Thomas and to his disciples, and said: "[?] me, that it is I. For a spirit does not have bones and flesh, as you see that I have."

92. Someone may argue cleverly: "But our Saviour's body was exceptional, because it alone was conceived from Mary without a man's seed." Was Adam's body different from ours too, then, because it was taken from earth alone without a man's seed? But no one can say that or prove it.

Someone may again argue cleverly: "Christ's body alone rose whole, but ours is not itself raised; another is raised in its place." How then does Scripture say, "Christ has risen, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep"? It is one and the same body [?], the firstfruits of those who are raised. Let them learn how Christ became the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep, and not turn again to another error and think that the other Scriptures lie.
For before himself he raised Lazarus and the son of the widow at Nain. Elijah, too, raised a dead man, and Elisha raised two dead men, one while he was still alive and one after he was buried.

But those who rose died again, and they are waiting for the one universal resurrection. Christ, however, is "the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep," because having risen he "dies no more; death no longer has dominion over him," as it is written.

For he died once, enduring suffering for us because of our sufferings. Once he tasted death, "even death on a cross." The Word came willingly into death for our sake, so that by death he might put death to death.

The Word became flesh. He did not suffer in his Godhead, but he shared the suffering of his humanity. The suffering was reckoned to him while he remained beyond suffering, and death was reckoned to him while he remained in

immortality, or rather while he was wholly immortality. For he himself said, "I am the life." [?] Nor does our hope come through flesh. For it says, "Cursed is the one who hopes in man, and he shall be like the wild tamarisk."

93. What shall we say, then? Is Christ not a man? From what has been said, it is plain to everyone that we confess without any doubt that the Lord, God the Word, became man not in appearance but in truth.

But he was not a man who came and advanced into Godhead. Our hope of salvation is not in a man, for no one among all the human beings descended from Adam could achieve salvation. Rather, God the Word became man, so that our hope might be not in a man but in the living and true God who became man.

"Every priest taken from among men is appointed on behalf of men," as it is written. So when the Lord came, he took flesh from our flesh, and God the Word became a man like us. In his Godhead he would give us salvation, and in his humanity he would suffer for us human beings, undoing suffering by suffering and putting death to death by his own death.

The suffering was reckoned to the Godhead, even though the Godhead is beyond suffering. It was reckoned to the Godhead because this is what the holy God the Word, who is beyond suffering, was pleased to do when he came.

Here is an illustration. Suppose someone is wearing a garment, and blood is spattered on it but does not reach the wearer's body. The bloodstain is still reckoned to the one wearing the garment. In the same way, in the

flesh Christ suffered, I mean in the Lord's man himself, whom the holy Word himself formed [for himself] when he came from heaven. As holy Peter says, "put to death in the flesh but made alive in the spirit," and again, "Since Christ therefore suffered for us in the flesh, arm yourselves also with the same mind."

Just as blood on a garment is reckoned to the one who wears it, so the suffering of the flesh was reckoned to him, to his Godhead, though the Godhead suffered nothing. This was so that the world might have its hope not in a man but in the Lord's man,

with the Godhead accepting that the suffering be reckoned to it. In this way salvation for the world would come from the Godhead, which is beyond suffering, and the suffering that took place in the flesh would be reckoned to the Godhead, though the Godhead suffered nothing. And so the scripture would be fulfilled that says, "For if they had known, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory," and so on.

94. So he was crucified, the Lord was crucified, and we worship the Crucified, who was buried, rose on the third day and ascended into heaven. "O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God," as it is written.

"For we know in part and we prophesy in part." It is as if we draw a drop from the ocean of the knowledge of God, and grasp only an illustration of so great a dispensation, the grace of our hope, given by the good pleasure of the Father and the will of the Son, together with the will of the Holy Spirit, [?] of the same dispensation of God.
All the Scriptures contained the proclamation of the resurrection here and there, but its fulfilment was reserved for the coming of the subsistent Word himself.

"For Christ is the fulfilment of the law," as it is written. Where in the divine writings is resurrection not spoken of? First Abel's blood proclaims it, for after his death "he still speaks," as Scripture says. "Enoch was taken up and was not found, and he did not see death, for he had pleased God." At God's command Noah built an ark, and so brought about a new birth for himself and his household.

Abraham in his old age receives a son, "his body being already as good as dead," and God granted hope out of the dead, all the more since "Sarah's womb" had been deadened. What had "grown old and was close to vanishing," the spring that had dried up of women's customary course, receives power again to conceive seed, and the old woman conceives like a younger one.
And Isaac was given back alive to his father out of death. In giving the boy back alive to his father, as though from the dead, God was proclaiming the hope of resurrection.

Jacob shows the matter too, for he did not treat the hope of his bones as secondary. He took care of them not as things that would perish but as things that would come back to life, and he gave careful instructions that they be carried back from the land of the Egyptians.

Joseph also signified this when he said, "Carry up my bones with you, for the Lord will surely visit you." If there were no hope of resurrection, why care about bones? Why should the righteous give instructions about bones that decay?

The first voice that came to Moses was God's testimony: "I am the God of Abraham and the God of Isaac and the God of Jacob," who sleep in the world but are alive with me. It is one and the same Spirit who spoke in the law and teaches in the gospel. The Saviour, who spoke in the prophets, indicated this to the Sadducees too. Behold,

95. let Aaron's rod show it as well. It was dry, perhaps for many years, and it was left in the tabernacle from evening until morning. Living trees bear fruit only with toil, over twelve months as the cycle of a year comes round, with the sun warming them, the rains watering them, the dews spreading over them, and night and day nourishing them.
But in a single night God made the difficult easy. The dry rod budded and put out leaves and ripe fruit. God was showing things like the resurrection that he will bring about.

When children are conceived in honourable marriage, which the Lord appointed, first the seed for succession is sown in the wombs that bring to birth, as the Lord ordained. As the time rolls on, what was sown in the belly is brought to completion over nine months. That is, what is conceived is perfected over nine months by count, and is born.

But it is not so in the resurrection, for the work is done in an instant. "For the trumpet will sound, and the dead will be raised imperishable." In the tabernacle of witness the Lord showed that the nuts which living trees carry for twelve months grew thick on the dry wood and shoots appeared, and in a single night. And not

only that: in the instant of one hour he accomplished what, as was said, takes twelve months. In the same way the infant that comes to be in the womb over nine months, being formed and perfected over a long time, is completed in an instant in the resurrection and rises.

96. Let the power of the Lord persuade the unbelievers, the Lord whose "will no one resists." Let Moses hear and demonstrate it. "What is in your hand?" says the Lord. He said, "A rod." This rod was wooden and certainly dry. And he says, "Throw it on the ground. And he threw" the dry rod.
And God made what was dry moist, and not only moist but alive, and changed in its nature, and formed differently in its substance.
The deed was no illusion. Truth is what works at God's command, not fantasy. In all things he corrected our understanding and brought it to the truth through Moses.
The prophet knew that what happened was not in appearance but in truth, as his flight shows. If he had known that what happened was an illusion, he would not have fled from the serpent.

But let this not become another stumbling block for the contentious, so that they say the rod was something else, "and God gave" it a different "body as he chose." First, let them learn that he did not bring one thing to life in place of another,

but brought to life that very rod which was dry. For God did not summon to judgment the body given to the rod, or the kind or form that moved through it, and he had no wish to judge the serpent in place of the rod.

Through the rod he provided assurance of the resurrection, and he displayed his own power, so that no one would disbelieve in his power in anything. And he did this with complete certainty. He did not raise some part of the rod, but changed the whole rod as he chose.

97. That these things are so, and that the dead have hope of eternal life and "those in the tombs will rise," call for me once more as witness the trustworthy Moses. When Reuben had sinned, his father, the holy patriarch Jacob, curses him and says, "Reuben, my firstborn and the beginning of my children, you ran riot like water; do not boil over. For you went up to your father's bed and uncovered it." (So it reads; in the Hebrew it is *elthothar*, which translated means "may you not return," or "may you not be added," or again "may you not excel"; but taken by the bare word it is "do not boil over," and the translators rendered it so.) And if you wish to learn that these things are so, and that death was decreed for him by his father because he had sinned, Moses will make it clear to you. For when he too was blessing the twelve tribes and came to Reuben, knowing that Levi was priest (for sins were loosed and bound by the hand of the priesthood), he says, "Let Reuben live and not die." But how could a man who had been buried a hundred and twenty-six years earlier live? But since Moses knew that the resurrection would certainly take place, and also knew the second death, the one that comes through condemnation on the day of judgment, he wished to spare him the things to come in return for the one punishment already suffered. So he says "Let him live" in the resurrection, signifying (for he knew that all will live) "and not die," that is, not be clothed with the second death that comes through condemnation and eternal torment. If he had been concerned about the loss of this life, it would have been enough to say only "Let Reuben live"; but since he is pointing to the things to come, he says, "Let Reuben live and not die."
98. And from where could one ⟨not⟩ gather a great many testimonies about our hope and expectation of the resurrection, a resurrection in truth and not in appearance?

Let the vainglorious, who quarrel to no purpose, tell us whether only a part of the body rises, and for everyone only in part, or whether for some the whole is raised, so that the resurrection is partial for some and of the whole body for others. What favoritism would that be? Is there "favoritism with God"? Certainly not.

Let us search out where or when the saints raised a dead person in part and not the whole body. The son of the widow in Zarephath rose whole, and no part was left behind; the son of the Shunammite woman rose whole, and not one of his limbs was left unrisen.

And the Lord raised Lazarus and left no remnant in the tomb, but [raised him] with the grave-bands and the rest of his wrappings * [?], and yet there will certainly be no need of clothes on the day of judgment.

He raised the son of the widow in Nain whole, and the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue, and the daughter of the centurion. How vain is the notion of those who reason that he raises part and leaves part behind!

Let us look at the facts before us, at what has already happened to us as a counterweight to our hope. Enoch was taken away whole and has not seen death to this day, and Elijah was taken up whole in the body and has not seen death to this day, so that in two living bodies God might show us the resurrection complete.

And so that no one might doubt, [he gave] two types * [?] in the two firstborn of our resurrection. Enoch was uncircumcised, and his uncircumcision did not hinder the resurrection or his body's receiving life through his way of living; Elijah was circumcised, so that the resurrection might not be thought to be for some and not for others, but wholly universal.

Elijah lived in virginity, so that the excellence of virginity might proclaim to the world immortality and incorruption with the body. But so that the resurrection and the body's continuance might not be thought to belong to virginity alone because of its distinction, Enoch was not a virgin, but self-controlled, and he begot children. And these two are alive, remaining in body and soul for the sake of ⟨our⟩ hope.

99. And again, so that no one might doubt, he brought others down to Hades with their bodies. The earth opened its mouth and swallowed Dathan and Abiram, the sons of Korah, and On, and they went down to Hades alive, ⟨with⟩ body and soul. From that very hour they were handed over to judgment: their bodies were not dissolved, nor was a remnant or a part handed over, but they were handed over whole, with body and soul,

to punishment. Job says, "until I come to be again," and "⟨may he raise up⟩ this body which endures these things," and "you will renew me," and again, "your youth will be renewed like an eagle's." And Isaiah says, "The dead will rise, and those in the tombs will be raised." For he is the one "who sets free those bound in might, and likewise those who provoke him, who dwell in tombs."

Job also says, "But a man who has fallen asleep will never rise again, nor will he know his place." And indeed the resurrection does not happen every day, but is appointed for a single day. And to show that he knew for what appointed time he was waiting, he immediately resolved the question: "until the heaven is no longer stitched together."

For as long as heaven and earth exist, the bodies remain in the earth. But when he comes who "rolls up the heaven like a scroll" and shakes the earth, then "those in the dust of the earth will also be raised."

That is why he says to Ezekiel, "Son of man, say that bone be gathered to bone and joint to joint," and so it happened; and "that sinews and veins, flesh and hair and nails come upon them"; and again, "Say, son of man: Come, spirit, from the four corners of the earth"—that is, from the places set apart as storehouses for souls.

And why does the Lord not speak himself, but command the man to speak? Because what the Lord says he also does at once, and it is never undone. He ordered the man to speak so that, once they had risen for the time being, our hope of salvation might be signified, yet it would be a man's word that was undone and not the Lord's. For those bones were going to die again. But when the Lord says, "Arise," they are raised and do not die, for the word of God will not be undone.

100. This is also why the Lord, having come in the flesh, raised the dead: so that what he raised through the flesh might fall asleep again, until the flesh itself rises and dies no more; and so that he might stop saying to one person alone, "Come out," until he comes and no longer says in the singular, "Arise," but "Arise, all of you," bringing about the universal resurrection. For he himself is the resurrection of the dead.

So after he rose from the dead he did not raise any of those who had recently died. For "many bodies of the saints who had fallen asleep rose with him and appeared to many," "having entered with him into the bridal chamber," as is written in the gospel.

And it did not say, "part of the bodies of the saints rose," but "bodies of the saints"; and "they appeared to many," not as other people than those who had died, but recognized by their own families, since they had died not long before.

Our Lord, wishing to show the wonder to others as well, performed these hard things in such a way as to show them to be easy. When he comes to the girl who had just died, the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue, since she had died that very hour, he deigned to say to her, "Child, arise," strengthening with the word "arise" what had already been dissolved, since she was still on the

bed. But the son of the widow in Nain, who was already being carried out on the bier, he raised more easily: "he touched the bier" and said nothing to the young man. He only touched the bier, and he rose.
And what is deeper still and far beyond human hope: when he came to Lazarus, four days dead, he did not even say "Arise," nor did he touch the tomb with his hand, but simply calls out readily, by his

own authority, "Lazarus, come out." "Come out" is much easier and readier than touching, and touching in turn is much easier than calling, "Child, arise." So the holy Word of God does all things in order to show us the hope of the resurrection.

101. If I wished to select ever so many testimonies from all the scriptures—small, limited, and unlearned as our mind is—still, because of their number, ⟨I fear that⟩ I would stretch the discourse to great length. To sum up, I will say that our salvation is concise, since in everything one hope, the hope of the resurrection, has been proclaimed to us.

These things the unbelieving disbelieve, the heretics corrupt, the contentious do not accept, and the vainglorious reject. But may God grant mercy to all and shine light into the darkened places of their thoughts.

For the pagans, having ⟨not⟩ received the Holy Spirit, will be refuted by the truth and by all the testimonies stated above, and above all by you, the sons of God's holy church and of the orthodox faith.

For you teach, having received the Holy Spirit and been counted worthy of "a fitting word in the opening of the mouth": first, that as disciples of Christ, counted worthy to be [disciples] of "the chief shepherd" and guardian of our souls * [?], gathering food for Christ's flocks, your own peoples, and taking care how you may nourish both yourselves and the things of God (I mean whoever truly wishes to be helped) from the holy land that is hinted at in Moses [?]...

Who among the right-minded, looking at you, the devout and faithful—O orthodox ones and sons of the church (in speaking of some I mean all who belong to the truth, as it is written)—who would have any doubt about these things?

For you are sons of a wise and most valiant woman, whose fame is in Solomon, who says, "Who will find a valiant woman?" as though she were rare, or rather unique. You will choose the better and love what is profitable.
By the valiant woman, I ask you, understand the church of God, your mother. Nothing is more valiant than she, who dies in every persecution raised against her for the name of her own husband.

102. This most gentle one, then, asks her own bridegroom earnestly in the book of the Song of Songs, "Where do you pasture your flock? Where do you rest at noon?" Christ pastures in the holy land mentioned before; and not only does he pasture, but he also commands the shepherds to loose the sandals from their feet, as he first says to Moses.

Having received this tradition from him, you yourselves also safely lead by the hand those who are first being introduced to holy knowledge, taking care that each one's sandals are loosed. And the sandals of each of us differ.

For each has shod himself with his own conduct. And so each one who obeys you, the disciples and good shepherds, has taken off at your admonition whatever he had put on: one idolatry, another adultery, another fornication, another theft, another greed.

And not only that, but renouncing hateful words and shameful talk for the sake of blessed hopes, each hands himself over, through you the good disciples, to be tended "under the mighty hand" of the good shepherd; for each will surely keep away from error.

And you set the truth before their eyes, exposing idols as counterfeits and openly proclaiming the error about them (for you do not even consider them dead, since they never lived), and rightly teaching everyone at all times that they are empty, vain, and nonexistent.

For they never existed so as to be anything. They are wretched things, an invention of the human mind that has strengthened the occasions for pleasure; and from there each person has dared to sanction his own passion as an object of worship.

For at the very first, when this novelty was introduced among men through the villainy of demons, it was declared "the first fornication," and idols were first sketched in shadow-paintings. Then each person handed down to his own children, as an object of worship, the very craft he practiced, by which he had secured his livelihood, and they fashioned gods out of the material of their own craftsmanship: the potter from clay, the carpenter from wood, the goldsmith from gold, and the silversmith likewise.

103. Further, each one portrayed his own passion in likenesses ⟩ of his own eyes [?]: the bloodthirsty man calling it Ares, the adulterer or adulteress the promiscuous Aphrodite, the tyrant giving wings to Victory.
The squalid man who gapes after the things of this life drew the image of Kronos; the effeminate man drew Cybele and Rhea—Rhea, I suppose, because of the flux of bodily promiscuity.
Another, a vagabond man or woman, fashioned Artemis the huntress; the drunkard, Dionysus; the toiler, Heracles; and the promiscuous man, Zeus and Apollo.

And why should I recount the multitude of countless passions found among human beings? The Egyptians, more deluded than all, not only worshipped their own passions, but "exchanged" the order of birds and four-footed beasts, land and water creatures, and certain wild animals, the very creatures the holy God had given them as servants.

Being beastlike in mind, they go to the extreme of impiety, deifying the animals of their country without shame: the dog, the barker; the cat, the eater of reptiles; the goat, the lecherous; the sheep, the bleater; the crocodile, the many-cleft [?] and most grim; the ibis, the eater of venomous creatures; the kite, the hawk, and the raven, most servile; and the snake, crooked and most loathsome.
In short, what great shame for those who neither perceive by sight what refutes them, nor take it in by sense, nor understand * [?] with the mind the vain things done among them!
So they are stricken with an evil fate, neither enlightened by their own philosophers nor joining as fellow spectators with those who ⟩ [?] the truth.

For they do not listen to Diagoras, who for lack of firewood burned his own Heracles, which was made of wood, and said to it mockingly, "Come now, Heracles, perform your thirteenth labor and come cook our dinner." He took it and split it, laughing at his own god as nonexistent, and joking, he ate the meal set before him.

104. Another, Heraclitus, says to the Egyptians, "If they are gods, why do you lament them?" (For they mourn Typhon and Osiris and other underworld beings with shrill dirges, as if they had been buried.) So he says, "If they are gods, why do you lament them? And if they are dead, you lament them in vain."

Another, a comic poet named Eudaemon, says, "If there are gods, I cannot speak about them or describe what sort of form they have; for there are many things preventing me." And Homer too says, "The rule of many is not good."
And Philemon, another comic poet, says, "Those who revere one God have good hopes of salvation."
Apis, the straw-eating calf, was struck on the thigh with a sword by Cambyses, king of the Assyrians, so that, if blood flowed, it might be proved not to be a god.

The worshippers of Kronos do not deny that their own god is shut up in iron chains; that is what they believe. But if someone is in prison, it is not simply because he is subject to someone greater, but because such a person is in prison as a criminal.
And if I am to speak also about * [?] Isis, who is also called Atthis and Io, daughter of Apis the Cappadocian, also called Inachus, I am perhaps ashamed to proclaim their deeds;

yet I shall not be ashamed to tell what they are not ashamed to worship. Let her worshippers and those of ⟨her⟩ lineage be ashamed, who urge their own daughters, wives, and sisters to imitate the deeds of the gods.

For straightway, in love with Osiris their own brother, and with Typhon the brother, they set their own brothers at war with each other. Great is the shame of a goddess who felt no respect even for her own brother, who in her lust was not content with men outside the family but went as far as her own brother.
And not only that, but through the insatiability of her desire she shows her dearest ones the way to fratricide.

And she bears Horus as a son, yet she could not establish who his true and legitimate father was. If she names Typhon, she is unsure whether he is not his parent; if Osiris, who could establish this with certainty?
Such a mother taught ⟨that he had become⟩ a fine god, after she had taken him with her and prostituted herself in Tyre for ten years.
And the people of Sinope, deifying as Serapis the king ⟨called⟩ Apis, served tyranny rather than truth.

105. These are the rewards of the gods honored among the Egyptians; to tell them in detail * [?] would use up much time. But the Greeks, who think themselves to be something, philosophizing only in words and sharpness of tongue and not in deeds, have run aground worse than all.

They derive Kronos from Ouranos, saying that he was begotten of Ouranos and [cut off] his own father's genitals (O wicked deed and shameful notion!); had his father not been castrated, there would have been many sons of Kronos's kind. And this noble fellow, who went so far as to attack his father,
was not content with his first impiety, but as a young man he wrongs his father, and when grown old, his own children,
swallowing Poseidon and Pluto, and searching for Zeus, and being tricked by Rhea, and swallowing a great stone wrapped in swaddling clothes instead of a baby.

As a god, no doubt * [?]. And being of noble parents, so to speak, his son, named Zeus, came near to becoming the husband of all women, and his son Hermes too. And would that he had become a lawful husband [?] according to the laws, and not always a seducer of other men's wives and an evildoer!
For he seduces Penelope, becoming a goat for the sake of pleasure; and he became a goat, I suppose, because of the vigor of his braided beard.

And to Danaë ⟨Zeus, the one we first named⟩ became gold, in order to seduce a chaste virgin shut up in her chamber. But he could never have become gold; rather, being a sorcerer, he bribed the virgin with gold and deceived her.
And with Leda he becomes a swan in turn, signifying the fluttering up of the fire of his pleasure.

And ⟨having become⟩ an eagle and flown up on one occasion, he presides as the teacher of corrupters of boys. Yet he never became an eagle; rather, sailing past Troy in a ship with an emblem, called Eagle for its speed, he seized Ganymede, the son of the king of the Trojans, and committed the defilement.
And to Pasiphaë he became a bull, and likewise to Europa.

106. And why should I tell the multitude ⟨of seductions⟩ of this noble seducer ⟨of virgins⟩ and teacher of seducers? His [tomb ?] is known to not a few: on the island of Crete, on the mountain called Lasios, it is pointed out to this day.

And there have been not one or two Zeuses, but three and four in number. One of them is the son of Kronos mentioned above, who cast his own father into Tartarus on Mount Caucasus; another is called Latiarius, from whom the gladiators arose; and another is the one of tragedy, who also burned his hand.

Perhaps, being a god, he forgot that fire bites, and lacked the foresight of the one who said to the goat, the satyr, who had first discovered fire and come up to kiss it: "Do not touch it, goat; if you touch it, you will burn your beard."
And there have been not one Athena but many: one who wandered and roamed about Lake Tritonis, another the daughter of Oceanus, another the daughter of Kronos, and many others.

There are many Artemises: one the Ephesian, another the daughter of Zeus, and likewise not a few others.
